a80.speaker: Baréma Koïta, Chief of the Ségou Fisheries Sector (Mali)
a80.speech: Said fish farming as a fish-breeding technique emerged in Mali through a small experimental station in the San Region, financed under a November 1979 agreement between Mali and the United States with USAID support, leading to an extension outpost being created in Niono ; detailed that the Ségou Circle currently has 131 ponds, 115 above-ground tanks and 2 floating cages, that rice-fish farming covers 7,500 m2 and that there are 31 ponds spanning 51.68 hectares, and that a 144 m3 floating cage produced 2,624 kg from 10,000 fingerlings while a 10 m3 tank with 1,000 fish yielded 369 kg ; stated that Nile tilapia and Clarias gariepinus are the two species studied, and named ongoing initiatives supporting fish farming in Ségou, including the Degraded Land Restoration Project (PRTD), a project supporting sustainable livelihoods for fishing communities adapting to climate change, and Jègè ni Jaba (JNJ).

a80.speaker: Baréma Koïta, Chief of the Ségou Fisheries Sector (Mali)
a80.speech: Said producers' access to inputs remains a concern, that his department lacks enough agents to cover the whole Circle, that growing insecurity hinders access to some localities, and that the service also faces a shortage of financial means ; said: "We must promote access to quality inputs at a reasonable price, have a permanent water source, regularly maintain infrastructure, and secure facilities against theft." Speaking about challenges and prospects, he mentioned reducing input costs, developing fish farming infrastructure, and strengthening producers' capacities.

a97.speaker: Joint Declaration (DRC, Rwanda, M23/AFC)
a97.speech: Issued by the DRC delegation, states that both parties agreed to end the conflict through peaceful means. The agreement emphasizes an immediate halt to hostilities, the categorical rejection of hate speech and intimidation, and an appeal to local communities to respect the emerging peace initiatives. Both sides pledged to engage in a constructive dialogue aimed at addressing the underlying causes of the conflict, particularly in the eastern provinces of the DRC. The statement also calls on religious leaders, civil society actors, and media organizations to help spread messages of peace. It states that dialogue will address the root causes of the conflict and establish mechanisms to ensure durable peace in eastern Congo.

a97.speaker: DRC representatives
a97.speech: Expressed sincere gratitude to Qatar for its efforts in facilitating the peace talks and for its continued commitment to fostering dialogue and mutual understanding.

a97.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a97.speech: Stated on X (formerly Twitter) that the declaration "paves the way for peace, stability, and prosperity" in the region, while safeguarding "strategic interest in critical minerals to grow our tech sector."

a97.speaker: Olivier Nduhungirehe, Rwanda's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a97.speech: Described the joint declaration as "an important — even decisive — step" toward achieving lasting peace in eastern Congo, provided that the commitments are implemented in good faith. Added that Rwanda remains engaged in other ongoing peace initiatives in the region.

a97.speaker: DRC government, Rwanda, and M23/AFC representatives (joint)
a97.speech: Urged continued support from local communities, regional stakeholders, and international partners to ensure the successful implementation of the agreement.

a211.speaker: Sunbird Tourism plc
a211.speech: Says its 2024 profit-after-tax increased by 102 percent to K10.6 billion courtesy of prudent cost management and revenue increase.

a211.speaker: Vilipo Munthali, Sunbird Tourism plc chairperson
a211.speech: Said the positive performance is despite foreign exchange shortage on the market and high cost of doing business: "The company has worked on several projects to rejuvenate our facilities. Most of them are old. At the same time, we are also trying to increase our offering by bringing new facilities, greenfield investments. Finance is a scarce resource and where it is made available to you, it costs an arm and a leg. And it's quite challenging in that respect."

a211.speaker: Vilipo Munthali, Sunbird Tourism plc chairperson
a211.speech: Said the change in US foreign aid policy is posing a risk of reduced business for the year 2025, adding that the economic environment is projected to remain volatile, while the upcoming election may offer opportunities to the hospitality industry, but with some interruptions that impact tourism, particularly in city hotels.

a211.speaker: Frank Harawa, general secretary, Minority Shareholders Association of Listed Companies
a211.speech: While commending the firm for the performance, said they are still hoping that Treasury will dilute its 71 percent stake in the hotel chain: "They could have given us 21 percent to increase ownership of the company by indigenous Malawians and raise capital for its projects."

a427.speaker: McHenry Venaani, Popular Democratic Movement leader
a427.speech: Believes the genocide agreement between Namibia and Germany is not about atoning for the atrocities committed against the Ovaherero and Nama people but a continuation of foreign aid: "The €1.1 billion that is being offered to the affected communities by the German government is equivalent to the amount that the German government has in any case donated to the Namibian government in foreign aid since our independence." ; "The proposed €1.1 billion, spanning over 30 years, is to all intents and purposes a continuation of foreign aid to a client state that Namibia is to Germany. It is not about atoning for the atrocities committed against the Ovaherero and Nama people."

a427.speaker: McHenry Venaani, Popular Democratic Movement leader
a427.speech: Said the "insignificance" of the quantum proposed by Germany cannot be any less than an affront to the affected communities: "For instance, in 2018, the German government set aside €1.1 billion for the production of battery cells for motor vehicles. Let us not forget that during the peak of the novel coronavirus outbreak, the German government set aside the same €1.1 billion as stimulus for the revival of the German arts and culture industry. Can we really argue that the immeasurable losses suffered by the Herero and Nama people can amount to the same budget given to the production of battery cells and the revival of the arts and culture industry in Germany? The answer is 'no'! This is a flagrant display of arrogance by the German government towards the affected communities and should not be construed any less."

a427.speaker: McHenry Venaani, Popular Democratic Movement leader
a427.speech: Accused the German and Namibian governments of having failed to comprehend and appreciate the damage of the colonial-era massacres of Ovaherero and Nama.

a427.speaker: McHenry Venaani, Popular Democratic Movement leader
a427.speech: Proposed that government renegotiate the terms of the whole genocide agreement, with parliament contributing robustly to the final agreement: "For this, we need to reinforce a stronger parliamentary role going forward." ; "In the same vein, the government must engage with the representatives of the affected communities both at home and in the diaspora. It is their birthright to be involved in these talks. Hence, the chant we heard during the recently held demonstrations against this very agreement was: 'Nothing about us without us!' – This rings especially true for the Nama and OvaHerero in the diaspora. They must be part of the story; just as they were part of the painful past."

a427.speaker: Affected communities and opposition parliamentarians
a427.speech: Have rejected the agreement, and protested last week as government was preparing to table the motion to debate the deal in parliament; hundreds of Namibians marched from Katutura to parliament to deliver a petition decrying the deal.

a427.speaker: Frans Kapofi, Namibian defence minister
a427.speech: Urged fellow lawmakers to remain calm when debating the contentious genocide agreement in parliament.

a427.speaker: German government
a427.speech: Acknowledged in May that it had committed genocide in colonial-era Namibia, after over five years of negotiating with Namibia.

a449.speaker: David Ricardo, English political economist (On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, 1817)
a449.speech: Cited as the source of the law of comparative advantage, one of the foundational principles in the theory of international trade, which “refers to an economy’s ability to produce a particular good or service at a…”

a526.speaker: Le Matin (Moroccan newspaper)
a526.speech: Reports that Guatemala reaffirmed its support for the Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara, described as the "only credible solution" to the conflict.

a526.speaker: Government of Guatemala
a526.speech: Reaffirmed its support for the Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara, describing it as the "only credible solution" to the conflict.

a526.speaker: Le360 (Moroccan news outlet)
a526.speech: Discusses a new strategy by the Office des Changes, with measures aimed at improving the business climate and strengthening financial transparency.

a526.speaker: El Watan (Algerian newspaper)
a526.speech: Reports a statement by the army chief of staff, Said Chengriha.

a526.speaker: Said Chengriha, Algerian army chief of staff
a526.speech: Recalls that general mobilisation is governed by law in the face of the "threats" weighing on the country.

a526.speaker: TSA (Tout Sur l'Algerie)
a526.speech: Announces the introduction of a new administrative requirement for importers, intended to better control trade flows in a tense economic context.

a526.speaker: Algerie360
a526.speech: Indicates that the former Minister of Communication, Mohamed Bouslimani, was sentenced to a term below the prosecution's demands in a corruption case, prompting mixed reactions.

a526.speaker: Mosaique FM (Tunisian radio)
a526.speech: Signals that junior doctors, interns and residents are close to a final agreement with the Ministry of Health, after several weeks of mobilisation.

a526.speaker: Tunisie Numerique
a526.speech: Notes an appreciation of the dinar against the dollar, attributed to the fall in demand for foreign currency and the recovery of transfers from Tunisians abroad.

a526.speaker: Libya Herald
a526.speech: Reports that the Central Bank and the National Oil Corporation (NOC) discussed an increase in oil production of 247,000 barrels per day, with the aim of generating 6 billion dollars a year to stabilise the Libyan dinar and support the country's economic balance.

a526.speaker: Egypt Independent
a526.speech: Revisits a meeting between Foreign Minister Sameh Shoukry and the American envoy David Satterfield, focused on a lasting ceasefire in Gaza and the delivery of humanitarian aid.

a526.speaker: Ahram Online
a526.speech: Indicates that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is about to finalise the 3rd and 4th reviews of its loan programme to Egypt, a crucial step for unlocking a new tranche of aid.

a553.speaker: Sunday Oduntan, Chief Executive Officer of the Association of Nigerian Electricity Distributors (ANED)
a553.speech: Has condemned what he described as a shocking display of military aggression at the headquarters of Ikeja Electricity Distribution Company (IKEDC) in Lagos ; speaking on Arise Television on Friday, said the incident occurred around 7:35am when multiple trucks carrying more than 100 fully armed Air Force personnel stormed the area from the Sam Ethanan Air Force Base in Ikeja. "The operation was reportedly led by the Air Officer Commanding, an Air Vice Marshal," he said. "We are very, very traumatised," he said. "I had a meeting in Ikeja yesterday, so I went there early because the management was preparing to attend the commissioning of a solar power plant in Ugutet. Suddenly, we saw military trucks arriving with heavily armed personnel. They stormed the premises, brutalising everyone in sight, including pregnant women. They forced workers to lie on the ground and assaulted them." ; "To fully understand how we have reached this level of lawlessness, it is important to look at the events leading up to this situation. This must stop," he stated.

a553.speaker: Sunday Oduntan, Chief Executive Officer of the Association of Nigerian Electricity Distributors (ANED)
a553.speech: Asserted that among the injured was the Chief Technical Officer of Ikeja Electric, who remains hospitalised, the same official responsible for managing the Air Force Base's power supply; explained that the conflict between IKEDC and the Nigerian Air Force stems from unpaid electricity bills dating back to November 1, 2013.

a553.speaker: Witnesses at Ikeja Electric headquarters
a553.speech: Reported that employees and others in the office were being beaten by the military personnel.

a553.speaker: Electricity billing records (IKEDC)
a553.speech: Records indicate that the Air Force Base at Ikegaya accrued a ₦7.56billion electricity bill between 2013 and 2022 but paid only ₦4.3billion, leaving a ₦3.2billion deficit. "In 2023, the base was billed ₦1.4 billion and paid ₦1.2 billion, while in 2024, its bill increased to ₦1.5 billion, but only ₦623 million was paid. This brought the total outstanding debt to ₦4.34 billion as of March 2025."

a553.speaker: IKEDC officials (Ikeja Electricity Distribution Company)
a553.speech: Claim the Air Force consistently refused to clear its arrears, even though funds were allocated for the purpose; that IKEDC attempted to resolve the dispute amicably by introducing an auto-recloser, but Air Vice Marshal A.K. Ademulegun rejected the proposal, insisting on 24-hour electricity despite non-payment; and that when IKEDC proposed the installation of prepaid meters the Air Force allegedly ignored official requests and denied IKEDC access to install the meters in December 2024.

a553.speaker: Ikeja Electricity Distribution Company (IKEDC)
a553.speech: Further accused the Air Force of vandalising its infrastructure, stating that military personnel tampered with an auto-recloser device twice, disconnecting communication cables in an act of sabotage; has since written multiple letters to the Chief of Air Staff and AOC Logistics, demanding accountability and immediate payment of outstanding debts.

a553.speaker: Air Vice Marshal A.K. Ademulegun, Nigerian Air Force
a553.speech: Rejected the proposal of an auto-recloser, insisting on 24-hour electricity despite non-payment.

a569.speaker: Mulambo Haimbe, Zambia’s Foreign Minister
a569.speech: Warned diplomats against interfering in the country’s affairs, saying there was an “increasing tendency” by envoys to ignore diplomatic channels, and this could undermine the “spirit of mutual respect”; said that addressing the government through the media amounted to interference and was in breach of diplomatic conventions ; “We remain open to addressing any matters of concern through appropriate diplomatic channels.”

a569.speaker: Michael Gonzales, US Ambassador to Zambia
a569.speech: Called a press conference to announce that the US was cutting $50m (£37m) of health aid to Zambia because of the theft of life-saving medications that the US had provided for patients; added that he had decided to go public after holding more than 30 fruitless meetings with senior Zambian officials; said that an inspection carried out by US officials at more than 2,000 pharmacies last year had found that most were selling drugs and medical supplies donated by the US.

a569.speaker: Michael Gonzales, US Ambassador to Zambia
a569.speech: Said the recent US measure was separate to the foreign aid freeze announced by President Donald Trump in January.

a569.speaker: US Embassy in Zambia
a569.speech: Said it had presented its findings of the alleged corruption to Zambian officials in April last year, and had offered help to stop further theft and to bring the culprits to justice; however, no action was taken by the Zambian authorities, it added ; the US accounts for about a third of public health spending in Zambia, according to the US embassy.

a569.speaker: Jacob Mwiimbu, Zambia’s Home Affairs Minister
a569.speech: Said that a forensic audit on the alleged theft had been completed and handed over to security agencies for further action, and that about 75 people have been arrested in a countrywide crackdown that saw more than 400 health facilities raided over the alleged scam ; “There will be no sacred cows in this pursuit.”

a569.speaker: Elijah Muchima, Zambia’s Health Minister
a569.speech: Earlier said the problem of theft predated the current government, which took office in 2021; also said several Zambian officials had been sacked following the thefts identified by the US, and that “an advanced digital stock tracking system” had been set up to monitor the supply of medicines ; reassured Zambians that there were sufficient stocks of all drugs so there was “no immediate risk of shortages.”

a569.speaker: Hakainde Hichilema, President of Zambia
a569.speech: In March said Trump had “slapped us on both cheeks”, saying it was time for his country to strengthen its treasury to procure its own medicines.

a634.speaker: Xi Jinping, President of China
a634.speech: Stated in his remarks at the 2024 FOCAC Summit that the friendship between China and Africa endures across time and space, mountains and oceans, and is passed down through the generations.

a966.speaker: Dalitso Kabambe, UTM President
a966.speech: praised the CCAP Synod of Livingstonia for maintaining independence in its operations, despite being founded by missionaries; said he hopes both the country and its politicians can learn from the church’s example by reducing dependence on foreign aid ; speaking during the Synod’s 150th anniversary celebrations in Mzuzu, noted that missionaries sought to fight greed, selfishness and slavery; said that while slavery was abolished, greed and selfishness remain and have fueled nepotism and tribalism in the public sector ; commended the church for its continued role in the fight for a better Malawi.

a967.speaker: Gertrude Torkornoo, suspended Chief Justice of Ghana (statement of case)
a967.speech: says President John Mahama acted arbitrarily in his decision to suspend her from office because of the three petitions calling for her removal on grounds of stated ‘misbehaviour’ and ‘incompetence’; according to her, the decision to suspend her in the absence of a reasoned prima facie determination constitutes a flagrant violation of the 1992 Constitution and the principle of fairness; she argues that the process governing the potential removal of the Chief Justice must be conducted with utmost circumspection and fidelity to constitutional safeguards, including rigorous adherence to substantive due process and administrative justice ; the statement of case argues that President Mahama’s failure to carry out a proper prima facie determination to a quasi-judicial or judicial process before suspending her violated constitutional provisions, including fairness and the exercise of discretion; it also avers that the Chief Justice has a right to challenge the validity of the President’s prima facie determination; she argues further that a prima facie determination devoid of any reasoning is no determination and that the terse statement from the Presidency announcing that a prima facie case had been established does not amount to a constitutionally compliant decision.

a967.speaker: Gertrude Torkornoo, suspended Chief Justice of Ghana (statement of case)
a967.speech: is also challenging the constitutionality of the committee and the decision by the President to appoint Justice Gabriel Scott Pwamang as Chairman and Justice Samuel Asiedu as a member; she claims Justice Pwamang had heard issues raised by two of the petitioners and Justice Asiedu was part of a panel that part-heard an application challenging the petitions; according to her, the argument is not that no Justices of the Supreme Court may serve on such a Committee, but rather that only those Justices who are not in any way directly or indirectly connected to the subject petitions or related proceedings may lawfully do so: “The sanctity of impartial adjudication and the institutional integrity of the Judiciary requires no less” ; further states that the failure of the three other members of the committee, Daniel Yaw Domelevo, Major Flora Bazaanura Dalugo and Prof. James Sefah Dzisah, to take and subscribe to the Judicial Oath prior to participating in the proceedings is a fatal breach of a constitutional and statutory requirement, rendering their participation unconstitutional and the committee improperly constituted ; on the public hearing of the proceedings, argues that since it is her rights, reputation and office that are directly at stake, she must be deemed to have the constitutional right to waive the in-camera requirement, seeing as the petitions and her responses have allegedly leaked to the public and been discussed on several platforms.

a967.speaker: Presidency of Ghana (statement)
a967.speech: a terse statement from the Presidency announced that a prima facie case had been established.

a992.speaker: Likando Kalaluka, State Counsel and former Attorney General of Zambia
a992.speech: Paid tribute to the late President Edgar Lungu, recalling both his personal humility and major policy achievements that often went unrecognized, and described their first collaboration in 2001 on the Law Association of Zambia’s work.

a1249.speaker: Moustapha Mohamed Mahamoud, Djibouti’s Minister of National Education and Vocational Training (MENFOP)
a1249.speech: Welcomed the “results obtained at this stage, which are already convincing and allow us to think that not only are we on the right track but that the objectives of the project have been fully achieved.” ; restated his full confidence in “this initiative, which is a cardinal programme on which we are counting greatly to rely on in order to bring significant improvements in teaching and learning in our schools,” hence his call for each of the actions undertaken to lead to tangible results and bring perceptible improvements in pupils’ performance in order to win the battle for quality, which remains a primary objective.

a1249.speaker: Jonathan Pratt, US Ambassador to Djibouti
a1249.speech: Shared the minister’s views and recalled that the DEGRA project aims to improve pupils’ reading performance in basic education from the 1st to the 5th year in the country, and is the tool par excellence for achieving this objective through three intermediate results: improving the quality of reading teaching and learning, increasing community participation in reading in basic education, and strengthening reading teaching and learning policies.

a1249.speaker: Panellists from MENFOP, parent-teacher associations (APE), school management committees (CGE) and civil society organisations (OSC)
a1249.speech: All acknowledged the clear strengthening of the capacities of the APEs and CGEs to carry out school and extracurricular reading activities, including awareness-raising on the importance of reading and how to support it through school projects.

a1249.speaker: Parents of pupils (APE members)
a1249.speech: Were particularly pleased with the mobilisation and full community involvement around the DEGRA project, which won the enthusiasm and support of everyone; the better supervision and the training given to teachers were also widely praised.

a1263.speaker: Gebeyehu Adugna, president of the Federation of Farm, Plantation, Fishery & Agro-industry Trade Unions
a1263.speech: "We've been left hanging," said Gebeyehu Adugna. ; Gebeyehu said they plan to help negotiate the collective agreement between the management and workers through the board.

a1263.speaker: Alemu Kora, Chairperson of the Derba Flowers workers' Association
a1263.speech: Said the management had refused to give medical care to employees who have been in labour. "They said they're running low on budget," he told Fortune. ; According to Alemu, most workers at the farm are finding it difficult to make ends meet with their inadequate salaries covering long distances to their workplaces at their own expense with low wages. He said that since most of the workers on the farm are women, security risk entails more prominent. "Workers have been subdued to imperious and ill-treatments," he said.

a1263.speaker: Tigist Ayenachew, Assistant Farm Manager, Derba Flowers
a1263.speech: Disclosed there has not been anything going on. "There's nothing to be concerned about," she said.

a1263.speaker: National Health Institute (report)
a1263.speech: Report indicated, from a walk-through survey performed on three flower farms several years ago, that flower farm workers have high prevalences of respiratory and dermal symptoms. Limited access to protective equipment and unsafe pesticides subject workers to adverse health effects.

a1263.speaker: Ashenafi Kora, Mullo Farm Workers' Association chairperson
a1263.speech: "Nothing has improved," said Ashenafi Kora. ; According to him, workers have been covering long walks to the farm and getting sick amid work as they cannot afford to take transportation and medical services with their low wages.

a1263.speaker: Tekalign Ayalew (PhD), head of the labour regulation and welfare services at the Ministry of Labour & Skills
a1263.speech: Said they have not received any letter concerning the flower farms. He said that regional problems are addressed by the Labour & Social Affairs Bureau. When the concerns prevail, the Ministry will comprise an inspection team to evaluate the concerns first-hand through negotiation. However, he disclosed the management will be questioned if they persist in not following the collective agreement rules. "The Ministry hands assistance during court procedures," Tekalign told Fortune.

a1263.speaker: USAID (report)
a1263.speech: USAID report indicates that workers in the flower industry are paid "shockingly" low wages, citing the government's policy to attract foreign investors by pointing at cheap labour as one factor.

a1263.speaker: Tilahun Girma, researcher and consultant at Abameda Consulting Plc
a1263.speech: Observes the benefits of providing transportation services should be granted according to the employer's will if it wishes to increase the productivity of its workers. According to Tilahun, labour exploitation of workers in the flower industry can only be seen through the lens of minimum wage, and since there is no minimum wage, it will be difficult to tell if workers are taken advantage of. However, he argues, mentioning the labour law, that employers must provide medical care if employees have been injured during labour hours. "It's a violation of labour law," he said.

a1273.speaker: Reports (on Saudi-Russian investment)
a1273.speech: According to reports, the total revenue of the companies into which the funds have been channelled has already totalled more than ₽4 trillion. ; In December, it was reported that Saudi Arabian investors, together with the Russian Direct Investment Fund, may invest ₽1 trillion, or almost $11 billion, in Russian projects over the next two years.

a1273.speaker: Business representatives from Middle Eastern countries at the International Economic Forum «Russia - Islamic World: KazanForum» (2023)
a1273.speech: noted such advantages of investing in Russian projects as «growth of the Russian market», «favourable conditions in special economic zones» and partnership relations of the countries that «allow large-scale investments».

a1273.speaker: Experts
a1273.speech: also drew attention to additional opportunities in regions of Russia where Islam has traditionally been widespread, such as in the Republic of Tatarstan.

a1273.speaker: Eljevit Oktem, director of the Russian enterprises of the holding company «Joshkunoz Alabuga»
a1273.speech: «For Turkish investors, I see advantages here both in lending and language - Tatar is similar to Turkish, specialists can easily understand each other. Therefore, our investments will continue»

a1273.speaker: KazanForum participants from the United Arab Emirates
a1273.speech: identified the main sectors of Islamic investment in Russia: wholesale trade and distribution, agriculture, transport and logistics, food production, construction services and other manufacturing, as well as halal tourism.

a1273.speaker: Rustam Minnikhanov, Rais of the Republic of Tatarstan
a1273.speech: said, during his recent visit to Iran, that the sphere of Islamic finance is becoming another important area of co-operation with the Islamic Republic of Iran - a traditional active participant of KazanForum.

a1299.speaker: Mouneissa Tandina, Malian drummer
a1299.speech: "My brother played with the Super Biton. He was Salif Keïta's drummer. He died in Ségou; I remember the song titled Mandjou, on which he was the drummer."

a1299.speaker: Mouneissa Tandina, Malian drummer
a1299.speech: "My mother was my first supporter. She saved all my earnings. Through the Super Biton orchestra, alongside Yéyé Koumba, I was spotted by several music personalities such as the late Toumani Diabaté, the late Mangala Camara, the late Ali Farka Touré, Cheick Tidiane Seck, etc."

a1299.speaker: Mouneissa Tandina, Malian drummer
a1299.speech: Expresses her regrets: "Indeed, after more than 30 years of a career in the service of music, I have still not received any distinction from the Malian authorities as a sign of recognition. Most of the famous artists with whom I began my career seem to have forgotten me. I fought against prejudice and played with so many celebrities who have cast me into oblivion. I did 17 concerts with Oumou Sangaré; I have always been at Cheick Tidiane Seck's side. The late Toumani Diabaté had promised me many things, but after his death I cannot get hold of his son Sidiki Diabaté. I have even performed in the theatre. The Germans made a documentary about my career and visited me at home; they were even astonished about me," she admits with a wounded heart.

a1304.speaker: Omar van Reenen, project manager and co-founder of Equal Namibia
a1304.speech: “This project is about more than art – it's about reclaiming drag and ballroom as part of African cultural heritage and using performance as a radical act of resistance in a time of escalating anti-LGBTQ+ laws.”

a1304.speaker: Androgynus Alpha, Kenyan fashion designer and activist, founder of Nadharia CBO
a1304.speech: “Drag and Vogue Beyond Borders is not just creating art – we're archiving a movement.” ; “It's about visibility, dignity and joy in the face of oppression.”

a1398.speaker: US Embassy in Tanzania (press statement, 19 December 2024)
a1398.speech: Stated that the plan is a continuation of the US Government's health assistance to communities affected by cholera outbreaks in Tanzania; that through the USAID clean-water project the US has provided Sh591 million ($250,000) to each region (Simiyu and Mwanza) and deployed technical water, sanitation and hygiene teams to support the respective regional health offices; that since September 2023 cholera cases in Tanzania have risen, with more than 2,200 people reported ill and more than 40 deaths; and that CDC is providing water purification tablets to people living with HIV and leading control efforts at PEPFAR-supported facilities: "The United States continues to support efforts to expand access to clean water and improved sanitation systems as a foundation for healthy lives and prosperity for all Tanzanians."

a1398.speaker: Andrew Lentz, US Chargé d'Affaires (Acting Ambassador) to Tanzania
a1398.speech: "Our rapid action demonstrates our commitment to saving lives and reducing the spread of cholera in Tanzania." ; "The United States will continue to be a close partner in strengthening Tanzania's health systems, including promoting access to clean water and environmental sanitation, which are essential in fighting this preventable disease."

a1415.speaker: Georgia Wallen, World Bank Country Manager in Liberia
a1415.speech: Says the report finds that a "business-as-usual" scenario in the country would yield only modest growth that is insufficient for achieving middle-income status by 2030 and substantially reducing poverty, a broad objective of Liberia's development agenda, the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development (AAID). By contrast, a high-ambition reform program shows potential for game-changing outcomes, many of which are linked to investing in the Liberian people and unlocking constraints to private and public investments. ; "With ambitious reform, Liberia could attain lower middle-income status before 2040, with improved jobs and a better quality of life for Liberians nationwide," she said.

a1415.speaker: Georgia Wallen, World Bank Country Manager in Liberia
a1415.speech: "Lessons learned and analysis of comparator countries like Ghana, Sierra Leone, Guinea, and Senegal, helps illuminate the pathways facing Liberia," she said, thanking attendees for joining in the launch of the Liberia Country Economic Memorandum. She noted that the report examines Liberia's development story and focuses heavily on actions that can shape Liberia's future, and that it draws from analysis of Liberia's peer countries to support accelerated results and help shorten the learning curve. ; "We hope this report will be a tool for policymakers, academia, students, think tanks, and interested Liberians - at home and abroad - to gain insights that can spur action."

a1415.speaker: Georgia Wallen, World Bank Country Manager in Liberia
a1415.speech: "First, why does this report matter for the AAID? Liberia's new national development plan for 2025 - 2029 aims to lift the incomes of Liberians by around 25% in five years - a bold aspiration. While that is ambitious, the AAID's aims actually go far deeper". Ultimately, the AAID is attempting to "reset" Liberia's development model - from "resource export" to emphasizing "sustainable value addition, processing, and innovations." ; "What will that take? What are viable - and necessary - pathways to a more prosperous future for all Liberians?" she quipped rhetorically. "This is where the analysis in the CEM comes in. As you'll hear today, the report sets out five key transitions that the country will need to tackle to unlock constraints to tomorrow's Liberia - including better quality of life, jobs, and diversification for long-term growth."

a1415.speaker: Georgia Wallen, World Bank Country Manager in Liberia
a1415.speech: Expressed optimism that while transformation may not come easily, it is possible. Sustainable, inclusive high growth will require strong policy action - and a whole-of-Government approach backed by strong commitment and accountability for results, she asserted, adding: "In today's session, you'll hear about short-term; medium-term; and longer-term policy actions needed to stimulate true transformation." She also noted that this ranges from boosting domestic revenue mobilization and enhancing public expenditure management in the short run, to diversifying away from an excessive reliance on mining over the medium/long-term. "One thing is clear. These next five years will be decisive for shaping Liberia's longer-term economic outlook."

a1415.speaker: Georgia Wallen, World Bank Country Manager in Liberia
a1415.speech: Assured government that as a longstanding development partner, the World Bank Group stands ready to support Liberia's "reset" and the ambitious strategic re-orientation reflected in the AAID. "This will underpin our support for the AAID and our forthcoming new World Bank Group Country Partnership Framework, which is in advanced stages of preparation." "We believe in the future of Liberia because we believe in the people of Liberia. We hope today's session will inspire action and stimulate informed dialogue."

a1768.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a1768.speech: "God has blessed your country. Go back and hold your corrupt leaders accountable. Stop loitering in the streets of America. If Americans were docile and refused to initiate Revolution, then you would never see such an amazing nation like USA... Stop depending on WHO for subsidized drugs. At your age, you ought to have home-made drugs for common ailments. On that ground, America has left WHO... Go and hold your ruling class accountable for rots in health care delivery. When they are sick, they run to USA for treatment with your national resources... America belongs to Americans not indians, Nigerians, Chinese, Mexicans, and other nationals who want good life and escaped to USA... Return to your country and change the narratives. No more running to America with your heavily pregnant wives. You want them to give birth in America and automatically become citizens of America. That is revoked immediately... Remain in your country and enjoy the consequences of being docile."

a1769.speaker: African Development Fund / African Development Bank Group (announcement)
a1769.speech: The African Development Fund has approved a 4.02 million euro loan with a grant component to finance the Government of Madagascar's 30 million euro equity investment in the Sahofika hydropower project, which will generate affordable, clean energy benefitting some 8 million people.

a1769.speaker: Government of Madagascar
a1769.speech: The government has committed to plough back the returns from the project to reduce electricity tariffs for the people of Madagascar.

a1769.speaker: Dr. Kevin Kariuki, African Development Bank Vice-President for Power, Energy, Climate Change & Green Growth
a1769.speech: "The support to the Sahofika project exemplifies the Bank's commitment to delivering quality, affordable energy access across the continent for sustainable and inclusive growth, while helping member countries to responsibly harness their vast, yet underdeveloped renewable energy resources. As the largest hydro power project under development in the country, the Sahofika project will unlock Madagascar's hydropower potential, and diversify its energy mix in favour of renewable at 90%."

a1769.speaker: Mohamed Cherif, African Development Bank Country Manager for Madagascar
a1769.speech: "The Sahofika project is a cornerstone of the Bank's strong support to the power sector in Madagascar. The commissioning of Sahofika would enable national utility (JIRAMA) to save around 100 million euros annually in fuel costs, while phasing out the need for state subsidies."

a1888.speaker: Father Santino Wise, Catholic priest in Tambura town, Western Equatoria
a1888.speech: Described the situation in the area as miserable, following the closure of the only market in the area due to deteriorated security in the County. Said the closure of the Tambura market more than a month ago has caused a severe humanitarian impact. He said that the market was shut down due to the deteriorating security situation in Tambura County, which has left residents struggling to access essential goods like food, medicine, and other daily necessities. “We are suffering a lot in Tambura County. Now I can say it's been going on for one month, there's no market, and even no food, no water, and no drugs. And people are not going to cultivate because of the issue of insecurity,” he said in an interview with Eye Radio ; says that with the market closed, local families are reportedly facing shortages, high prices, and growing desperation.

a1888.speaker: Father Santino Wise, Catholic priest in Tambura town, Western Equatoria
a1888.speech: Called for an urgent need for restoration of peace and security, as well as humanitarian assistance to support those trapped in the worsening crisis: “People are not living in their houses, those plastic shelters which was giving since 2021 are the once still in the IDP's camp of Tambura with a lot of rains, now people are suffering and children also, we are crying to our national government, and for those who are listening to our voices, so we are crying a lot. We talk a lot, and there's no change, now even there's sugar and soap, and now we are sending our voices to be heard,” he appealed.

a1959.speaker: Kobenan Kouassi Adjoumani, Minister of State, Minister of Agriculture, Rural Development and Food Production of Côte d’Ivoire
a1959.speech: Stated on 21 February 2024, at the press conference launching the 2024 cashew season, that local processing of cashew nuts recorded an increase of 94% from 2021 to 2023, explaining that this performance is due to “28 active units which processed 265,863 tonnes of raw nuts, representing 22% of national production, compared with 224,036 tonnes in 2022 and 136,854 tonnes in 2021 (14%)” ; he said this success is also to be credited to the Cotton and Cashew Council and to specific support measures for cashew processors decided by the government.

a1959.speaker: Kobenan Kouassi Adjoumani, Minister of State, Minister of Agriculture
a1959.speech: Welcomed the fact that in 2023 Côte d’Ivoire was able to export 50,200 tonnes of kernels to some fifty countries around the world, compared with 36,807 tonnes in 2022, an increase of 36%: “This makes our country the world’s 2nd largest supplier of cashew kernels after Vietnam, in addition to being the world’s 3rd largest processor of cashew nuts.”

a1959.speaker: Kobenan Kouassi Adjoumani, Minister of State, Minister of Agriculture
a1959.speech: Specified that these figures should keep rising given the entry into operation of processing units expected in 2024, and said the expected level of processing should rise to 320,000 tonnes compared with 265,863 tonnes in 2023, a forecast increase of 20%; he recalled that the objective remains the local processing of 100% of production.

a2426.speaker: John Mahama, President of Ghana
a2426.speech: Has called for a united Africa to enable the continent to address its escalating debt crisis, adding that unsustainable borrowing risks undermining development gains and sovereignty ; delivering a keynote speech at the African Union (AU) High-Level Conference on Debt in Lomé, Togo, described Africa’s debt burden as a “paradox of need and vulnerability,” with countries spending more on debt servicing than on health and education combined ; “Let us act not as debtors pleading for relief, but as partners demanding reform. Africa, united, can turn debt into opportunity.” ; “Debt can be a catalyst for transformation, but it can also be a source of fiscal fragility and lost sovereignty if not well managed.”

a2426.speaker: John Mahama, President of Ghana (citing IMF and AfDB data)
a2426.speech: Citing data from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the African Development Bank (AfDB), said 22 African nations were at high risk of debt distress, while the debt-to-GDP ratio in sub-Saharan Africa had surged from 40 per cent in 2015 to over 60 per cent in 2025.

a2426.speaker: John Mahama, President of Ghana
a2426.speech: Reflecting on Ghana’s situation, said that while the country reduced its debt from 100 per cent to 30 per cent of GDP under the HIPC initiative in the early 2000s, reckless borrowing and external shocks, including COVID-19 and global inflation, pushed debt back to 90.7 per cent by 2022 ; said interest payments alone consumed 47 per cent of the government’s revenue in 2023, describing the country’s $5.4 billion debt restructuring deal in 2024 as a critical but “painful” step towards recovery ; outlined three key lessons from Ghana’s experience, emphasising the need for timely creditor engagement to prevent deeper crises, aligning multilateral support with domestic priorities, and ensuring debt sustainability through strong governance rather than just focusing on ratios.

a2426.speaker: John Mahama, President of Ghana
a2426.speech: Proposed a three-pillar continental strategy to tackle the debt challenge: stressed the importance of transparency, noting that less than 40 per cent of African nations published detailed debt reports; advocated productive borrowing, urging African countries to focus on high-impact sectors such as agriculture, renewable energy and digital infrastructure; and called for global financial reforms, demanding fairer credit ratings and expanded roles for African institutions such as the AfDB and Afreximbank ; urged African leaders to explore innovative solutions such as debt-for-climate swaps, modelled after Barbados, to fund green projects, as well as green and blue bonds for sustainable development ; emphasised the need for stronger tax systems and domestic capital markets to reduce reliance on foreign loans.

a2426.speaker: John Mahama, President of Ghana
a2426.speech: Criticised the slow progress under the G20 Common Framework, noting that only three of the five African applicants had seen tangible debt relief and therefore called for faster and more equitable restructuring processes ; rallied his colleagues to adopt a Common African Position for the 2025 G20 Summit, establish standardised debt transparency benchmarks across the AU, and fully operationalise the African Monetary Institute and the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) to boost intra-African trade.

a2582.speaker: Council of Ministers of Mali
a2582.speech: announced that the Malian government adopted several decrees on Wednesday aimed at structuring and securing the artisanal mining sector, following several deadly accidents that occurred in illegal gold mining sites.

a2582.speaker: Local sources
a2582.speech: said a collapse on February 15 at the Bilaly Koto site in the Kayes region caused the death of at least 48 people, mainly women.

a2600.speaker: Monrovia City Corporation (MCC)
a2600.speech: Said the training is a gesture from the Government of India through the Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation Program of the Ministry of External Affairs of India; officials of the Corporation said the beneficiaries are expected to undergo several weeks of intensive training in various fields related to the function of their departments.

a2600.speaker: John-Charuk Siaffa, Monrovia City Mayor
a2600.speech: Said the MCC under his administration is focused on restructuring and reforming the Corporation through intensive capacity-building opportunities; lauded the Government and People of India for the opportunity; admonished the employees to be passionate and take the training seriously; revealed that scores of international capacity-building opportunities are in the pipeline for deserving MCC employees; “The MCC under my watch will provide you with the tools and capacity you need to drive the vision of making Monrovia better.”

a2600.speaker: Two of the beneficiaries (departing MCC staff)
a2600.speech: Spoke on behalf of the departing staff and lauded the Mayor for giving them the opportunity to hone their skills at some of the best-performing universities in India; expressed excitement about the unprecedented opportunity and assured the Mayor of their commitment and unflinching support to promote the vision of transforming the MCC.

a2664.speaker: Farmers in the Kunene and Omusati regions of Namibia
a2664.speech: Say non-functional abattoirs and poor livestock infrastructure are primary obstacles to accessing a profitable market. This issue surfaced during the ongoing oversight visits by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Economics and Public Administration in the Northern Communal Areas (NCAs). Many farmers in the area feel that they are being deliberately sidelined in the marketing of their livestock, and have repeatedly appealed to be allowed to graze their animals in the quarantine camps, particularly during droughts.

a2664.speaker: Lisha Empowerment and Development (2022 petition to the National Assembly)
a2664.speech: Urging the revival of the livestock market in the NCAs and parliamentary intervention to address the sector's severe underdevelopment. The petition calls for urgent action to rejuvenate the livestock market in the NCAs, with concerns about the market's decline into near extinction.

a2664.speaker: Farmers in the Oshana Region
a2664.speech: Have also joined the growing chorus of condemnation against the cordon veterinary fence, which they say is discriminatory.

a2664.speaker: Ministry of Agriculture, Water, and Forestry (following discussions)
a2664.speech: Following discussions with the Ministry of Agriculture, Water, and Forestry, it was revealed that the government is implementing infrastructure improvements, including constructing and upgrading abattoirs and meat processing plants in Katima Mulilo, Rundu, Oshakati, Eenhana, and Outapi.

a2664.speaker: Timotheus Kativa, Meatco representative
a2664.speech: Said that there are plans to resume operations via commodity-based trade, buying livestock from Omusati region farmers for local quarantine before transporting them to Meatco's export abattoirs in Rundu and Katima Mulilo.

a2736.speaker: Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPCL)
a2736.speech: Said on Monday that discussions are currently ongoing towards emplacing a new naira-for-crude contract with local refiners ; while clarifying the development said it has noted recent reports circulating on social media regarding the alleged unilateral termination of the crude oil sales agreement in Naira between NNPC and Dangote Refinery.

a2736.speaker: Olufemi Shoneye, Chief Spokesperson of the NNPC
a2736.speech: “To clarify, the contract for the sale of crude oil in Naira was structured as a six-month agreement, subject to availability, and expires at the end of March 2025.” “Discussions are currently ongoing towards emplacing a new contract. Under this arrangement, NNPC has made over 48 million barrels of crude oil available to Dangote Refinery since October 2024. In aggregate, NNPC has made over 84 million barrels of crude oil available to the Refinery since its commencement of operations in 2023.” “NNPC Limited remains committed to supplying crude oil for local refining based on mutually agreed terms and conditions…”

a2736.speaker: Sources (unnamed)
a2736.speech: Said this was due to “irreconcilable” differences bothering on product delivery and other issues.

a2736.speaker: Dangote (no comment)
a2736.speech: There was no official comment yet from Dangote on the reported collapse of the naira for crude deal.

a2736.speaker: Source close to the Dangote refinery (anonymous)
a2736.speech: Confirmed that it is true that the deal collapsed; he did not provide further clarification.

a2736.speaker: Document reviewed by Daily Trust (late January)
a2736.speech: Indicated that for February 2025, the scheme has been allocated only four cargoes, and for March, just two cargoes totalling 950,000 barrels (1.9 million barrels in total for the month), representing an allocation of 61,290 barrels per day – far below the 385,000 bpd target under the scheme.

a2736.speaker: Nigerians, experts and marketers
a2736.speech: Said the arrangement ordered by the president was responsible for the relative stability recently recorded in the foreign exchange ; said the development would further trigger depreciation of the naira, resulting in an increase in prices of petroleum products.

a2736.speaker: Akinrinade Akinade, petroleum industry player
a2736.speech: Warned that the development would affect the prices of petroleum products and called for the intervention of President Tinubu who initiated the scheme in the first place: “I read it like you. It has not been confirmed yet. It was the President that ordered the NNPC to do it. It is not final” ; according to him, the scheme was felt largely “in the value of naira to dollar” ; “It was one of the reasons the dollar had some air space. If that one changes, we might see another devaluation of the naira because the refineries would have to be looking for dollars to source their crude. This will also affect the price of petroleum products.”

a2736.speaker: Adetunji Oyebanji, industry player and marketer
a2736.speech: Said the deal was not sustainable ab initio because of the forward contracts the federal government had committed to, and stated that the only solution was to increase crude production to 2.5m barrels daily from the present 1.7m: “I am sure all of you are aware that they (NNPC) have committed a lot of their crude for the loan that they took initially at the beginning of this administration. So, they have committed a good portion of the contract… Not only NNPC but the IOCs (International Oil Companies), a lot of crude they produce to banks for facilities and so on… So, when they started talking about this crude for naira, I was wondering how they are going to succeed? Where are they going to get the crude from? Unless you increase the crude production to about 2.5m barrel a day, you would never find the extra crude to give to local refineries. That is the only solution.”

a2736.speaker: Tunde Kugbeha, analyst
a2736.speech: “Anyway the Tinubu’s directive to conduct crude oil transactions in naira, is to strengthen the local currency, reduce dependence on the U.S. dollar, and ease pressure on Nigeria’s foreign exchange reserves. By reversing this policy, the NNPC is effectively reinforcing dollar demand, which could further weaken the naira maybe to N2000 this time and with food being cheap now we should expect to be paying more.” ; “The official reason given is that the NNPCL has already committed its crude production to forward contracts, leaving no supply available for domestic refiners under the naira-for-crude arrangement. However, this raises concerns about whether the policy was properly implemented… If the government is serious about promoting the use of the naira, there may need to be a policy review or direct intervention to ensure that domestic refiners can access crude in local currency as originally planned. Otherwise, this move could undermine confidence in government policies and fuel further instability in the forex market.”

a2736.speaker: Adeusi Anthony, lawyer
a2736.speech: Said the decision would impact on the value of the naira, saying, “NNPC’s decision to switch back to selling crude oil in dollars instead of naira is a major policy reversal…” ; “When they first introduced naira payments, the idea was to boost the local currency, which I considered to be a very good policy, it was meant to ease pressure on forex demand, and improve liquidity in Nigeria’s financial system. But in reality, it seems like challenges such as naira instability and hesitation from international buyers made the shift difficult to sustain… By returning to dollar transactions, NNPC is likely trying to make crude sales smoother, and attract more buyers. However, this could put more pressure on the naira and Nigeria’s forex reserves. In the long run, building investor confidence is paramount… I still think, though, that the best idea in my modest opinion is to leave the erstwhile policy as it were, for the long term interest.”

a2796.speaker: Joint Oversight Committee (US, Qatar, Rwanda, the DRC, Togo — the African Union facilitator — and the African Union Commission)
a2796.speech: Met for the second time to review the deal in Washington DC, noting with grave concern the “slowness” in the implementation of the agreement. They also raised concern about the escalating violence in eastern DRC, in violation of a ceasefire agreement.

a2796.speaker: M23 representatives
a2796.speech: Say they have shown willingness to find a lasting solution to the conflict, accusing Kinshasa of sabotaging peace processes.

a2796.speaker: Democratic Republic of the Congo government
a2796.speech: Justifies its snub of the dialogue by arguing that M23 is a terrorist organisation as declared by the United Nations and the AU, and accusing Mbeki of favouring Rwanda and the Kigali-backed rebel outfit.

a2938.speaker: President Rupiah Banda of Zambia (speech read by Vice-President George Kunda)
a2938.speech: Warned that there will be no sacred cows in the fight against corruption; assured the nation that the amendment of the Act had ensured that the fight against corruption had been strengthened. Said section 38 of the ACC Act now covered everyone both from the public and the private sector as opposed to section 37 which only targeted civil servants. "There are no sacred cows in the fight against corruption and as we fight corruption, we also do soul-searching of ourselves," he said. ; Said if a member of the civil society pays a civil servant to steal a document which is later given to a newspaper then that would be fighting corruption using corruption. ; Said what the Government had done was to harmonise the laws and that they were now up to international practice because when amending Section 37 of the ACC Act research was conducted and it was not different from what obtains in Britain and other countries.

a2938.speaker: President Rupiah Banda of Zambia (speech read by Vice-President George Kunda)
a2938.speech: Said Zambia was also making arrangements for the pending United Nations Convention Against Corruption (UNCAC) peer review mechanism and that Transparency International Zambia was involved in the process; said in line with UNCAC the country had launched the National Anti-Corruption Policy (NACP) to coordinate the corruption fight and that a national steering committee chaired by the secretary to the Cabinet had been put in place to oversee the implementation; said to achieve the desired results it would require that all Zambians took interest in anti-corruption work and support various institutions and individuals involved in the implementation of the NACP.

a2938.speaker: President Rupiah Banda of Zambia (speech read by Vice-President George Kunda)
a2938.speech: Said the institutionalising of the fight against corruption through integrity committees was a sign of Government's desire to eliminate corruption through promotion of transparency and accountability leading to improved public service delivery; said integrity committees had been set up at 17 institutions and were not limited to public institutions but had been extended to private companies such as Konkola Copper Mines; said in 2008 the Government launched the public service code of ethics to instill professionalism in the public service; said the Government would continue to strengthen the ACC and other governance institutions in order to meet the UNCAC demands, and had strengthened the Prohibition and Prevention of Money Laundering Act and enacted the forfeiture of proceeds of Crime Act to enhance the recovery of stolen public resources.

a2938.speaker: Millennium Challenge Corporation report
a2938.speech: Indicated that Zambia had made progress in controlling corruption; the progress had been assessed as having improved from 71 per cent in 2009 and 74 per cent in 2010 to 77 per cent in 2011 although there was more work to be done.

a2938.speaker: Godfrey Kayukwa, ACC Director General
a2938.speech: Said the commission was satisfied there were now sufficient legal provisions to deal with public officials, private individuals and corporate bodies that engaged in corrupt practices ; said the fight against corruption required the involvement of head of State, senior Government officials and the people including civil society organizations.

a2938.speaker: Viola Morgan, United Nations Development Programme country director
a2938.speech: Said that corruption was a scourge that should be addressed because it affected fundamentals upon which the nation was built.

a2938.speaker: Trevor Nyoni, ACC Copperbelt regional manager
a2938.speech: Has called for concerted effort from all stakeholders in the fight against corruption; said following Government's launch of the implementation plan of the national anti-corruption policy which aims to harmonise strategies in the fight against corruption, there was need for participation of all stakeholders in its implementation in order to realise the desired results. He was speaking in Kitwe during the commemoration of the International Anti-Corruption Day activities.

a2957.speaker: Mamadou Traoré, representative of the governor of Bamako
a2957.speech: Strongly praised Orange-Mali's initiative, declaring: “This donation symbolizes our collective commitment to supporting vulnerable populations by easing their suffering and giving them hope. The donations allow them to meet their urgent needs. This gesture illustrates the fundamental humanitarian values: solidarity and mutual aid.” ; addressing the beneficiaries, he said: “we are aware that this assistance will not cover all your needs, but it represents a first step toward easing your suffering. It attests to our determination to leave no one behind and to remain at your side in the face of the challenges you are confronting.”

a2957.speaker: Fatogoma Aristide Sanon, deputy managing director of Orange-Mali
a2957.speech: “Each kit is made up of a tarpaulin for shelter, a 25kg bag of rice, 2 impregnated mosquito nets, a 2-person mat, a blanket, a 20-litre plastic bucket, a kettle, 2.1 kg of soap and 1 feminine hygiene kit. Added to these kits are clothing, sheets, shoes, and a symbolic cash envelope collected by all of Orange-Mali's staff for the benefit of the flood-affected families. The total cost is valued at more than 55 million CFA francs, of which more than 52 million was disbursed by the Orange-Mali Foundation in order to strengthen the resilience of our compatriots affected by the floods.” ; He said this distribution of donations constitutes the second phase of Orange-Mali's support to the affected populations, after an initial gesture of the same kind worth 10 million CFA francs, and that it adds to other activities already carried out by the Orange-Mali Foundation as part of its philanthropic work, with an investment of more than one billion CFA francs since the beginning of 2024.

a2957.speaker: Orange-Mali Foundation
a2957.speech: Explains that through this gesture it wants to express its generosity and solidarity toward Malian populations in disadvantaged situations.

a3005.speaker: German Embassy in Juba, in partnership with WFP in South Sudan
a3005.speech: Pledged to continue providing humanitarian assistance to needy populations including Sudanese refugees but said the government needs to shoulder responsibility; highlighted the impact of Germany's support in conflict and climate-affected areas in South Sudan following a four-day visit to Upper Nile State.

a3005.speaker: Amb. Deike Potzel, Director General for Crisis Prevention, Stabilization, Peace Building and Humanitarian Assistance at the German Federal Office
a3005.speech: Described the humanitarian situation in Renk and Malakal in Upper Nile State as dire and needing serious intervention; assured German support for South Sudanese returnees and Sudanese refugees in terms of humanitarian assistance ; "While we stand ready to support South Sudanese people, we also urge the government to take full responsibility for humanitarian and the people in it, accountability is essential in this regard and it is important we join hands all together, the humanitarian, the development agencies and the peace actors to join efforts with government and local authorities to understand the need of the people."

a3005.speaker: Rania Dagash Kamara, WFP Assistant Executive Director for Partnerships and Innovation
a3005.speech: Applauded the German partnership with the World Food Programme in providing support for humanitarian assistance in the country; commended South Sudanese for what she terms their "generosity" for hosting the Sudanese refugees despite the hardships ; "Accommodating a million of people who have crossed a border, even as returnees or refugees in a time when we know many of them are vulnerable and need assistance themselves, is nothing short of commendable and truly signals that humanity is a link between the communities. So, it is a great appreciation from us the World Food Program to the people of South Sudan."

a3149.speaker: United States government
a3149.speech: Has reaffirmed its commitment to support Zambian farmers practicing Smart Farming Practices in the face of the drought that has been declared a disaster, having devastated six of the country’s 10 provinces.

a3149.speaker: Michael Gonzales, U.S. Ambassador to Zambia
a3149.speech: Said his Government would continue working directly with farmers to improve productivity, nutrition, and livelihoods, while the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) and government finalise plans on a massive grant to support agriculture-related infrastructure ; confirmed that the U.S. government would this year invest more than K500 million (US$20 million) in funding for agriculture, environment, and climate adaptation.

a3236.speaker: Josep Borrell, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy
a3236.speech: Denounced at a press conference in Cairo: "We almost made it, but we did not [achieve the ceasefire]. Why? Very simple, because those who promote war have no interest in ending it. They are pretending, less and less, because their intransigence is accompanied by impunity and their actions have no consequences." ; Warned that "flagrant violations of international law continue to be ignored" by Israel, recalling that the EU had "unconditionally" supported the mediation efforts of Egypt, Qatar and the United States for a ceasefire in the Gaza Strip, something that "has been announced so many times" without success ; "If institutions such as the International Criminal Court [ICC] are threatened, if the decisions of the International Court of Justice [ICJ] are completely ignored, then what is the solution and whom can we trust?"

a3236.speaker: Josep Borrell, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy
a3236.speech: Indicated that the EU will spare no effort in supporting a ceasefire, which must be accompanied by a "political solution" to the historic conflict, the release of the hostages held by Hamas and the guarantee of humanitarian support for the Palestinians ; said that "a process must be launched" to implement the two-State solution, as well as "to understand what kind of pressure should be exerted on those who do not want this solution," referring to the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

a3236.speaker: Josep Borrell, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy
a3236.speech: Said that "no one has done more than the European Union" to financially support the Palestinian National Authority and the humanitarian situation in Gaza since the start of the war on 7 October: "No one can say that what we do in the region is just good intentions. We are the largest donor to the PNA. These are not intentions, they are millions of euros: we have been the largest donor in support of humanitarian aid in Gaza. It is more than 300 million [euros] since the beginning of the war." ; "The EU is supporting Palestine at every level to alleviate the suffering of the punished population of the Gaza Strip." ; "Please, do not say that it is only an illusion. Look at the accounts, look at the flow of money, look at the number of flights landing at the airport carrying humanitarian aid to the people of Gaza. Is anyone doing more than we are?"

a3236.speaker: Arab press
a3236.speech: Accused the European bloc of "double standards" in the Gaza conflict.

a3236.speaker: Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, President of Egypt
a3236.speech: Stressed to Borrell the responsibility that falls on the international community and the EU to "exert intense pressure to reach an agreement that puts an end to the ongoing war" in Gaza.

a3494.speaker: Tobacco Industry and Marketing Board (TIMB)
a3494.speech: According to the TIMB, Zimbabwe has already sold over 300 million kg since opening in March - surpassing its previous record of 296 million kg set in 2024.

a3494.speaker: Leonard Chimwaza, agriculture expert
a3494.speech: Identifies three primary challenges undermining Malawi's competitiveness including declining global tobacco prices, intensifying competition from other producers, and unequal international market conditions: "European Union subsidies to European tobacco farmers distort the global market. Countries like France, Germany, Spain, and Greece receive direct support that often exceeds the average auction price of tobacco here in Malawi. This makes it extremely difficult for our farmers to compete on level terms."

a3494.speaker: Velli Nyirongo, economist
a3494.speech: Highlights the structural challenges facing Malawi's tobacco sector, noting its fundamentally buyer-driven nature where companies dictate purchase volumes, provide inputs to contracted farmers, and largely determine pricing mechanisms; he also points to shifting global consumption patterns, where demand for traditional leaf tobacco is stagnating while alternatives like e-cigarettes and heated tobacco products gain market share. "This operates as a demand-led market. Farmers don't grow to supply an open market - they grow to fulfil specific contracts, with very few operating independently." ; "Malawi has yet to break into these emerging markets." ; "Even with this year's bumper crop, the country still cannot meet full buyer demand."

a3494.speaker: Rhodes Sulumba, Vice President of the Tobacco Association of Malawi Trust
a3494.speech: Reiterated that while the market is functioning well, price levels have disappointed farmers: "So far, we can see the market is going on well and the prices have at least improved but it's not as much as compared to last season's prices. Normally everybody wants good prices and looking at the prices this year, the prices are a bit lower compared to last season. We will at least achieve last year's earnings due to the fact that this year we grew a lot of tobacco not because of the prices."

a3591.speaker: United Nations
a3591.speech: says the world is forgetting Sudan, where civilians are caught in a civil war; on Wednesday urged countries not to forget the civilians caught up in the war in Sudan, appealing for $4.1 billion to meet their humanitarian needs and support those who have fled to neighbouring countries.

a3591.speaker: United Nations
a3591.speech: According to the UN, half of Sudan's population - around 25 million people - need humanitarian assistance and protection, while more than 1.5 million people have fled to the Central African Republic, Chad, Egypt, Ethiopia and South Sudan.

a3591.speaker: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a3591.speech: in the launch of its joint appeal with the UN refugee agency (UNHCR), called for $2.7 billion in funding to provide humanitarian aid for 14.7 million people.

a3591.speaker: UN refugee agency (UNHCR)
a3591.speech: asked for $1.4 billion to support nearly 2.7 million people in five countries neighbouring Sudan as part of the appeal.

a3591.speaker: Martin Griffiths, UN aid chief
a3591.speech: told diplomats at the United Nations in Geneva: "Sudan keeps getting forgotten by the international community." ; "There is a certain kind of obscenity about the humanitarian world, which is the competition of suffering, a competition between places: 'I have more suffering than you, so I need to get more attention, so I need to get more money.'" ; said the international community needed to act with a heightened sense of urgency: "We must not forget Sudan. That's the simple message that I have to say today."

a3591.speaker: Martin Griffiths, UN aid chief
a3591.speech: told reporters the warring sides had been invited to Geneva to discuss how civilians can access aid; said the parties had agreed in principle, but the details of any meeting still needed to be worked out.

a3698.speaker: Kyongsig Park, Korean Ambassador to Ghana
a3698.speech: Has described his country’s longstanding relationship with Ghana as one founded on genuine friendship with no strings attached ; said that the Korean government’s investment in the country was driven by the mutual friendship between the two nations, adding that they were not in the business of demanding favours from Ghana in exchange for investments ; said their investments in Ghana were a gratuity for the immense support it enjoyed from the international community during its recovery from the Korean War ; “So, we come here as a friend and provide Official Development Assistance (ODA) as a friend. It is not a transactional thing. Our diplomatic relations and cooperation in the international forum are based on our friendship,” he said ; further stated that the two countries shared similar political experiences, including colonisation and military takeovers before their final transition to a democratic system.

a3698.speaker: Kyongsig Park, Korean Ambassador to Ghana
a3698.speech: Said approximately $43 million had been allocated for ODA projects across various sectors including health, education, agriculture and environment in the country ; added that his government and Ghana signed an agreement last year to provide $2 billion concessionary loans through the Korean Exim Bank to support Ghana’s development programmes ; “We are focusing on Ghana because the country is very safe and stable. We share the same values, such as democracy and market economy. That is why Ghana is usually called the beacon of democracy in Africa. ‘’We deeply respect that, especially considering the country had a peaceful election last December. It was very impressive to me,” the ambassador said.

a3698.speaker: Kyongsig Park, Korean Ambassador to Ghana
a3698.speech: Said the two countries have maintained steady trade relations of over $200 million U.S. dollars annually, however Korea’s exports to Ghana are greater than Ghana’s exports to Korea ; said that the Korean government, through the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency (KOTRA), had invited many Ghanaian businesses to various trade fairs in Korea ; “KOTRA has also provided information about products the Ghanaian side can import and gives good explanations about the economic situation in Ghana to the Korean businessmen who have good intentions of investing in Ghana. With this effort, I believe our trade and investment will increase in the future” ; added that as part of his country’s broader interests in the development of Africa and its intra-trade relations, he had also offered support to the Africa Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), and “this year, we will provide $4.5 million to AfCFTA for the projects.”

a3851.speaker: Two top government officials (anonymous)
a3851.speech: confirmed on Saturday that President Lazarus Chakwera has reportedly fired Reserve Bank of Malawi (RBM) Governor Wilson Banda, apparently after running out of patience with the man he appointed in July 2020.

a3851.speaker: A top Capital Hill official (anonymous)
a3851.speech: “It is true that he has been relieved of his duties. What I am not sure of is how the Office of the President and Cabinet [OPC] has handled the matter.” ; “It could be that he will be paid salary until the end of his contract or he is being paid a lump sum of his benefits for the remaining months.”

a3851.speaker: A well-placed State House source (anonymous)
a3851.speech: corroborated the President's decision to sack Banda, but said OPC was preparing a public statement on the issue.

a3851.speaker: Robert Kalindiza, OPC spokesperson
a3851.speech: said he was still consulting to provide a concrete position.

a3851.speaker: Moses Kunkuyu, Minister of Information
a3851.speech: did not respond to our questionnaire.

a3851.speaker: Anthony Kasunda, Presidential press secretary
a3851.speech: referred enquiries to Finance Minister Simplex Chithyola Banda.

a3851.speaker: Simplex Chithyola Banda, Finance Minister
a3851.speech: did not respond to our calls.

a3851.speaker: Wilson Banda, Reserve Bank of Malawi Governor
a3851.speech: declined to comment, stating: “I am not taking any questions or interviews from the newspapers. I know what you want to ask. Tikambirane sabata ya mawa zimenezo [let's discuss that next week].”

a3851.speaker: Wisdom Mgomezulu, economist and Malawi University of Business and Applied Sciences lecturer
a3851.speech: linked the governor's removal to failures to effectively execute policies. He pointed to the prevailing high inflation rates, exchange rate instability and missteps in currency revaluation as some of Banda's major performance issues ; “His administration's failure to address these issues worsened the economic crisis.”

a3851.speaker: World Bank
a3851.speech: says six percent growth is needed to meaningfully reduce poverty.

a3878.speaker: Joseph Boakai, President of Liberia
a3878.speech: Wants member states of the Mano River Union to invest in the empowerment and growth of the youthful population. President Boakai said: “Investing in the growth and improvement of young people remains pivotal to sustaining economic growth and development.” He admonished the heads of the MRU Secretariat to take practical steps in improving the livelihood of the young generation, and said the MRU as an institution must begin to prioritize programs and policies that aim to promote and protect the youthful population in the sub-region.

a3878.speaker: Joseph Boakai, President of Liberia
a3878.speech: Lauded the Heads of the Mano River Union Secretariat for work done over the years in ensuring the institution remains effective and functional.

a3878.speaker: Simeon Moribah, Head of the Mano River Union Secretariat
a3878.speech: Underscored the need for enhanced collaboration and partnerships in sustaining the organization. Mr. Moribah said: “The effective operations of the MRU can be achieved with the support of donors and partners. The MRU has benefited from the partnership forged with the UN, African Development Bank, and USAID, among others.”

a3878.speaker: Simeon Moribah, Head of the Mano River Union Secretariat
a3878.speech: Described the Liberian Leader['s visit] to the organization as historic and urged other heads of member states to follow suit.

a3878.speaker: Sara Beysolow-Nyanti, Liberia's Foreign Minister
a3878.speech: Reading the resolution on Tuesday, Minister Nyanti said: “Both nations also agreed on partnership to advance transformative initiatives in diverse sectors, to create opportunities for economic growth and development in the Mano River Union.” She quoted Presidents Joseph Boakai and Julius Maada-Bio of Sierra Leone as underscoring their dedication to unite the sub-region to create the necessary conditions to feed the people and create more jobs.

a3878.speaker: Joint communique / Resolution of Liberia and Sierra Leone (document)
a3878.speech: Liberia and Sierra Leone have a joint communique reaffirming their commitments to promoting cross border cooperation to boost the peaceful coexistence between border communities and cultural diversity, as well as economic activities; the two countries also agreed to support peaceful and democratic transition of power aimed at maintaining peace and security at the continental and international levels. According to the Resolution, the Heads of State also expressed their continued support to the principles of the African Union and United Nations, particularly on peace, security, and development.

a3933.speaker: Elon Musk, head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
a3933.speech: Has declared that USAID should “die”; branded USAID a “criminal organisation”; “Time for it to die,” Musk wrote on his social media platform X.

a3933.speaker: Multiple US media outlets, citing unnamed officials
