a3933.speech: Reported that USAID’s director of security, John Voorhees, and his deputy, Brian McGill, were placed on leave after denying DOGE personnel entry to secure areas over their lack of security clearances.

a3933.speaker: Steven Cheung, White House director of communications
a3933.speech: Denied that DOGE personnel had attempted to gain access to secure areas, calling a PBS report about the incident “fake news” and “not even remotely true at all” ; “This is how unserious and untrustworthy the media is,” Cheung said in a post on X.

a3933.speaker: Katie Miller, DOGE staff member
a3933.speech: Appeared to acknowledge the task force’s attempted entry, writing on X that “no classified material was accessed without proper security clearances”.

a3933.speaker: Chris Coons, Democratic senator for Delaware
a3933.speech: “President Trump spent two weeks harassing and laying off USAID employees, and now his team is trying to gut the agency altogether,” Coons said on X. “These are patriotic Americans who promote our leadership around the world. They make us safer. Trump makes us less safe.”

a3933.speaker: Jeremy Konyndyk, former director of USAID’s Office of US Foreign Disaster Assistance (2013-2017)
a3933.speech: Said that eliminating USAID without an act of Congress would be unlawful and a breach of the separation of powers enshrined in the US Constitution ; “If this gambit succeeds – if Trump (or Elon) can just override Congressional statutes and funding mandates, and Congress acquiesces – it’s a very dark sign … and it won’t stop at USAID,” Konyndyk said on X.

a3933.speaker: The New York Times and The Associated Press
a3933.speech: Reported over the weekend that DOGE had gained access to the federal payment system, which holds sensitive personal information about millions of Americans.

a3933.speaker: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, New York Congresswoman
a3933.speech: “This is a five alarm fire. The people elected Donald Trump to be President – not Elon Musk,” she said on X. “Having an unelected billionaire, with his own foreign debts and motives, raiding US classified information is a grave threat to national security. This should not be a partisan issue.”

a3933.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a3933.speech: Told reporters on Sunday that his administration would get the “radical lunatics” out of USAID before making a decision on its future.

a3933.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a3933.speech: Singled out aid to South Africa, pledging to cut off “all future funding” in response to land confiscations and what he said was the poor treatment of “certain classes of people” ; “The United States won’t stand for it, we will act,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, adding that the funding freeze would stay in place until a “full investigation of this situation has been completed”.

a3933.speaker: US government data
a3933.speech: The US allocated nearly $440m in assistance to South Africa in 2023, according to US government data.

a4056.speaker: Global Fund (Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria)
a4056.speech: has directed US$544,385,745, equivalent to 1.35 trillion shillings, to Tanzania to address these diseases over three years, 2024/2026; of that amount 711 billion shillings goes to HIV/AIDS interventions, 448 billion shillings to malaria and 101 billion shillings to tuberculosis – an 11 per cent reduction on the amount originally allocated for the seventh cycle.

a4056.speaker: Information obtained by Mwananchi (unnamed sources)
a4056.speech: Information Mwananchi obtained says the reduction of that support removes activities that consumed a lot of money but lacked value, including meetings, workshops and the purchase of vehicles in some areas, in line with the guidance issued by the Global Fund.

a4056.speaker: Ministry of Health of Tanzania
a4056.speech: said that owing to changes in the foreign policies of various stakeholders there has been a shortfall of funds in the financing of various sectors, and that the projects most affected in the health sector are those for AIDS, malaria and tuberculosis.

a4056.speaker: Dr Grace Magembe, Chief Medical Officer of the Government
a4056.speech: said that to ensure citizens continue to receive services without any obstacle, in the 2024/2025 financial year the Government allocated and disbursed 141.98 billion shillings to guarantee continuity of services, including the purchase of antiretroviral drugs (ARVs), and malaria and tuberculosis medicines. "For 2025/2026, the Government has allocated 158 billion shillings to enable the availability of services for these diseases, including the availability of medicines, reagents and essential equipment, up to June 2027." ; said that alongside allocating money to buy various commodities, the Government has also continued to issue employment permits for various health cadres, employing 13,564 health professionals between July 2024 and June 2025 and assigning them to work stations; and said the Government will continue to allocate funds every financial year according to the needs that arise.

a4056.speaker: UNAIDS report of 2023
a4056.speech: a report issued by the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) identified those areas as including epidemic diseases such as Covid-19 and mpox, the war in Ukraine and other disasters, which caused an economic downturn; the report showed that sub-Saharan African countries including Tanzania remain a major problem, accounting for a large share of new HIV infections at 59 per cent in 2021, that 38.4 million people worldwide were living with HIV in 2021 with 650,000 deaths from AIDS-related illnesses, and that 133 of 195 countries worldwide are at risk of lacking financial resources, with some 20 sub-Saharan African countries worst off, and young women and adolescent girls from those countries being infected every two minutes.

a4056.speaker: Dr Mugisha Nkoronko, President of the Medical Association of Tanzania (MAT)
a4056.speech: said the money from that fund has been contributing nearly 20 to 30 per cent of our health sector budget for a long time; said this is an alarm bell to wake us from the deep sleep of our planning as a country, so that our budget can be self-sufficient and not depend on donors and development partners. "We do not refuse development partners being present, but they should not decide the future of our lives; when they have withdrawn, the Government must have joint strategies and must call all stakeholders and organise to be self-reliant in the health sector."

a4056.speaker: Francis Luwole, National Coordinator, COMPASS Tanzania
a4056.speech: said the effects that will result from the reduction of that allocation are a major priority now, and that the focus is more on life-saving services such as follow-up and treatment; said social services such as education and strengthening health systems will not be a major priority from that fund, so they are going to decline. "Now if you look at HIV and AIDS, new infections are 60,000; if funds are reduced in the area of controlling new infections, we should expect infections to increase within the next few years, and the Government will again incur losses buying medicines and treating people." ; said the key thing is to change priorities, that as a country we should look at what we had before, prioritising things with big results using little money; said that to save costs it is important to integrate related services, because the global trend now is that donor funds will continue to decline, and it is the right time to build up domestic funds to tackle diseases. "We set priorities on which services, and we should not neglect social services and life-saving prevention. These are things to consider – HIV alone takes a lot of money; for many years we have depended on donor funding in this area by 90 per cent."

a4056.speaker: Dr Lilian Mwakyosi, Director of the Dare Organisation
a4056.speech: said that in this seventh cycle, which began on 1 January 2024, it was discovered in May this year that resources were already scarce and the allocation had fallen by more than 11 per cent, so it is time for the country to keep organising itself. "In HIV, malaria and TB interventions it has fallen by 11 per cent and we do not know what it will look like when we enter the eighth cycle in 2027/2029."

a4056.speaker: Dr Mwigulu Nchemba, Minister of Finance
a4056.speech: said on 12 June this year, while presenting the Government's 2025/2026 Budget, that these steps followed ongoing policy changes worldwide which have caused key development partners to reduce the assistance that was being provided for health services, including combating and controlling various diseases, especially AIDS; said the Government proposes to establish alternative sources of revenue in order to reduce the budget deficit caused by the decline in that assistance, by amending various laws. "It is proposed that 70 per cent of the additional revenue be directed to the AIDS Trust Fund (ATF) and 30 per cent be directed to the National Health Insurance Fund for All."

a4153.speaker: Representatives of Niger's Foreign Ministry and WFP Country Director Kinday Samba (statement)
a4153.speech: “They expressed gratitude to Russia for its contribution to the World Food Programme's operations in Niger, noting that this Russian assistance will cover three months' worth of sunflower oil consumption for vulnerable groups, including refugees,” the statement read.

a4206.speaker: Neal Rijkenberg, Eswatini’s Minister of Finance and Chair of the Bureau of the African Union’s Specialised Technical Committee on Finance, Monetary Affairs, Economic Planning and Integration
a4206.speech: Said this role is not about prestige but about advancing an ambitious agenda that seeks to shift Africa’s position in the global economy from primarily exporting raw materials to producing high-value goods within the continent: “I will be pushing an agenda for African governments to use their buying power to produce high-value goods on the continent” ; said the idea is simple: if African governments commit to buying African, they can drive demand for local industries, stimulate job creation, and keep more value within their economies ; said that by producing more high-value goods at home, Africa can retain wealth that currently leaves its shores ; “African governments spend billions annually on procurement. Imagine if a significant portion of that was channelled into factories and industries on the continent. The multiplier effect would be enormous.”

a4206.speaker: Neal Rijkenberg, Eswatini’s Minister of Finance
a4206.speech: Said, as he begins his tenure, that the key question is whether Africa can turn its rhetoric of economic independence into tangible results, and that the challenge is clear — to turn Africa’s buying power into a force that not only meets the continent’s needs but also positions it as a global economic player.

a4240.speaker: Iziaq Salako, Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Nigeria
a4240.speech: Has warned that malaria continues to strain Nigeria's economy and health system ; stressed that malaria remains “often underestimated and referred to as ordinary despite its devastating impact on individuals and communities.” ; “In Nigeria, malaria continues to be a major public health issue, with children under five years of age and pregnant women being most at risk.” ; “This disease not only causes suffering and death, but it also disrupts the economic ecosystem by hindering productivity and increasing healthcare costs.”

a4240.speaker: World Malaria Report 2024
a4240.speech: Cited by Mr Salako as attributing 27 per cent of global cases and 31 per cent of global deaths to Nigeria.

a4240.speaker: Iziaq Salako, Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Nigeria
a4240.speech: Under the administration's Rethinking Malaria Initiative, outlined a plan tailored to sub-national needs and backed by the newly established Advisory on Malaria Elimination in Nigeria (AMEN); he said this will harness top malaria experts across the globe to provide technical assistance and support for elimination efforts.

a4240.speaker: Iziaq Salako, Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Nigeria
a4240.speech: Announced nationwide rollouts of proven interventions to drive towards a malaria-free Nigeria by 2030: he said, this year, 12 states, including Kano, Kaduna, and Oyo, will receive fresh insecticide-treated nets, while “we will be implementing Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (SMC) in the 21 SMC-eligible northern states and providing approximately 30 million under-five children with malaria preventive medicines.”

a4240.speaker: Iziaq Salako, Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Nigeria
a4240.speech: Despite the freeze in USAID/PMI support, said Nigeria has stepped in to fill the gap and confirmed that the federal budget now covers essential commodities ; “To ensure last-mile delivery, an integrated supply chain mechanism, coordinated by the National Product Supply Chain Management Programme, will be utilised” ; “This will help to ensure efficient delivery of these life-saving commodities to where they are most needed.”

a4240.speaker: Iziaq Salako, Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Nigeria
a4240.speech: Further highlighted the role of the private sector; noted that the Nigeria End Malaria Council, chaired by Aliko Dangote, is mobilising corporate funding to support the implementation of the National Malaria Elimination Programme ; “By working together, we can improve access to equitable, affordable, and quality-assured healthcare products and services for malaria and make a significant impact in eliminating this disease from our country.”

a4240.speaker: Daju Kachollom, Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare
a4240.speech: Urged Nigerians not to trivialise malaria and encouraged early care at subsidised primary-health-care centres; highlighted environmental factors like climate change, insecurity and humanitarian crises that hamper elimination efforts, and called for stronger inter-ministerial coordination ; “The federal government has greatly subsidised the treatment of malaria, especially in the primary health care sector. So if you have malaria, please go to the primary health care sector.”

a4240.speaker: Onyebe Ella, Visual Artist and Social Inclusion Activist
a4240.speech: Explained that her virtual paintings draw on the personal loss of her elder brother who died of malaria, to “depict the realities of malaria in the country”.

a4363.speaker: Gerson Msigwa, Chief Government Spokesperson of Tanzania and Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Information, Culture, Arts and Sports
a4363.speech: Announced that the country’s upcoming general election, scheduled for October 2025, will be financed entirely by the Tanzanian government, not by foreign donors, and stated that the 2025/26 budget is a crucial one as it will allocate funds specifically for the election and will mark the completion of the National Development Vision 2025 ; “The most important thing for all Tanzanians is that we are going to present an election budget funded entirely with our own resources. This is something all Tanzanians should be proud of — our independent Tanzania, self-reliant and making its own decisions, must have a self-financed budget.”

a4363.speaker: CP Nicodemus Tenga, Commissioner of Legal Affairs and Prison Operations
a4363.speech: Stated that the Mama Samia Legal Aid Campaign has assisted over 12,000 inmates and remandees across the country’s prisons, among them 6,900 remandees released after receiving legal assistance; noted significant improvements in prison management, highlighting that the ratio of inmates to remandees has shifted from 50:50 to 75 percent inmates and 25 percent remandees due to the reduction in the overall prison population, which has decreased from over 32,000 in 2021 to 26,896 as of June 9, 2025 ; “Currently, the capacity of prisons is 29,102 inmates, but we have a shortfall of over 3,000 inmates, meaning there is available space in our facilities.”

a4363.speaker: Human Development Report 2023/2024, published by the United Nations Development Programme
a4363.speech: Reveals that African countries have the lowest Human Development Index (HDI) score, with only four of the 52 African countries ranked making it into the top 100, and indicates that the continent’s strong economic growth has not necessarily translated into improved global rankings.

a4376.speaker: The organisers (Sunbird Tourism plc Men’s Conference)
a4376.speech: According to the organisers, the event aims to bring together men from diverse backgrounds to share experiences and challenges they face.

a4376.speaker: Temwa Kanjadza, Sunbird Tourism plc head of sales, marketing and distribution
a4376.speech: Said they are committed to hosting events that promote personal growth, community building and social responsibility ; said the Men’s Conference aims to empower men to become their best selves through sessions and conversations with renowned speakers in their field of study ; “In a time where conversations around men’s mental health, emotional intelligence and positive masculinity are more important than ever, corporate involvement is a crucial enabler in building a culture where men continue to thrive” ; said they believe in investing in initiatives that create real change, including those that equip men with tools to lead healthy, balanced and purpose driven lives.

a4376.speaker: Pokani Kaunda, Vwaza Multimedia artist relations manager
a4376.speech: Said the Vwaza App exists to turn the craftsmanship of local music into revenue that can help artists achieve their goals ; “We look forward to more sign ups from different kinds of artists. We are here to make sure you are heard, differently and empowered in the process,” she said.

a4376.speaker: Lawi, Malawian musician
a4376.speech: Said he looks at the partnership with Vwaza Multimedia as a window to export Malawian businesses and a chance to give artists the support they need ; “Just because something is new, does not make it less irrelevant.”

a4376.speaker: Charles Kabena, public relations practitioner
a4376.speech: Speaking in an interview, said it is important to do away with some stereotypes which portray men as invincible beings and create a safe space where they can share experiences about their vulnerability to the world around them ; “We are living in a generation where things are changing and life has been changing as well. Today, as men we are confronted by so many challenges. If you look at economic factors things have been worsening. Back then, our parents used to have very stable jobs and incomes, but it is not the same with us today. The struggle is becoming huge across the genders. Our dreams are not being realised despite having people putting much effort.” ; said these spaces have to be structured to help men understand that they are not alone and not just to celebrate their masculinity, but also embrace their vulnerable parts of masculinity that have been created by our various social situations.

a4424.speaker: National Bank of Ethiopia (data)
a4424.speech: Data from the National Bank of Ethiopia reveals exports to Europe, which account for 38pc, is the major market for Ethiopian commodities.

a4424.speaker: Sisay Amare, president of the Ethiopian Pulses, Oilseeds & Spices Processors Exporters Association (EPOSPEO)
a4424.speech: Would like to see exports to China increase; reasoned that export earnings are not where they should be compared to the total number of people involved in the sector, accredited the underwhelming performance of the sector to logistics costs, and said the setting of price floors by the government also does not help in competing in international markets as someone could easily get an alternative seller somewhere in the world.

a4424.speaker: Oxford (estimate)
a4424.speech: Oxford estimates total financial commitments of 2.4 billion dollars, mostly in interest-free loans, up to the gear shift towards a more market-oriented relationship following Mao's era in 1976.

a4424.speaker: Stein Sundstol Eriksen, research professor (study presented at FSS/CMI seminar)
a4424.speech: Presented a study looking at how the relationship between China and Tanzania has evolved over the past 70 years.

a4424.speaker: John Magufuli, President of Tanzania
a4424.speech: Referred to the 10 billion dollars loan for port construction agreed upon by the previous administration as “terms and conditions only a drunkard would accept”.

a4424.speaker: Aslak Orre and Muhidin Shangwe, lecturer in the Department of Political Science & Public Administration at the University of Dar es Salaam
a4424.speech: Presented the cautionary tale of Mozambique, which is faced with a severe debt crisis, noting it averaged seven percent real GDP growth in the early 2000s, that its debt to GDP ratio reached 122pc in 2020, and that it borrowed heavily from external donors, particularly China, following the 2006 resource boom.

a4424.speaker: The researcher (report on Mozambique's hidden debt)
a4424.speech: Estimates the actual cost of the borrowing at around 11 billion dollars in reduced economic activity and dragged two million people under the official poverty line.

a4424.speaker: Gedion Jaleta, CEO of the Center of Excellence International Consult
a4424.speech: Embellished China’s economic engagement in Africa as ‘aid mixed with investment’; heralded China’s non-interference in politics as market and trade orientation while indicating that bilateral trade between Ethiopia and China has reached six billion dollars ; ascribed the responsibility in the management of loans to be falling in the hands of host governments, and said loans are not bad by themselves.

a4447.speaker: Abdoulaye Bio Tchane, Minister of State in charge of development, Chairman of the Board of Directors of MCA-Benin II
a4447.speech: According to him, the resolutions adopted will enable the MCA-Benin II coordination team to move surely and on schedule through the next steps towards the entry into force of this second compact ; In opening the session, he recalled how important this compact is, saying that, entirely devoted to energy, it constitutes a key means for development in Benin: "Today, the number one obstacle to economic growth is energy."

a4447.speaker: Samuel Batcho, National Coordinator of MCA-Benin II
a4447.speech: Said the team he leads is certain that, with the support of the Board of Directors and the MCC country team, the entry into force will be a success, envisaged for the first quarter of 2017 ; He recalled that in the process, the coordination team has, since the 3rd ordinary session of the Board, continued the preparatory activities for entry into force and the setting up of staff and their working framework.

a4789.speaker: Ministry of Infrastructure of Rwanda (via Business Insider Africa)
a4789.speech: Reports that 82% of Rwandan households now have electricity access, with 57% connected to the national grid and 25% relying on off-grid systems, primarily solar.

a4789.speaker: Experts
a4789.speech: Warn that this overreliance on hydropower leaves Rwanda vulnerable to climate shocks like droughts.

a4789.speaker: Kigali's Least Cost Power Development Plan (2024-2050)
a4789.speech: Aims to add nearly 1,500 MW of solar capacity with battery storage by 2050.

a4789.speaker: Government of Rwanda
a4789.speech: Estimates it needs $3.6 billion by 2035 to meet rising electricity demand, including $69 million for short-term solar projects, with long-term generation costs potentially surging to $38 billion by 2050.

a4789.speaker: Industry players
a4789.speech: Are calling for more predictable policies and cost-reflective tariffs, arguing that expanding incentives for private investors is crucial for meeting Rwanda's bold clean energy vision.

a4904.speaker: Ministry of Finance (MoF)
a4904.speech: Has promised to reduce and change the excise tax levied on bottled water manufacturers ; the government announced that it would amend the existing excise tax proclamation which had expanded the types of products that could be taxed and increased the amount of indirect tax, and also plans to reduce the tax percentage on some products and exclude others from excise taxes altogether.

a4904.speaker: Bottled water industry representatives
a4904.speech: Had frequently asked the government to reconsider the excise tax imposed on bottled water production.

a4904.speaker: Ashenafi Merid, General Manager of the Ethiopian Bottled Water and Soft Drinks Manufacturing Industries Association (EBWSDMIA)
a4904.speech: Said that via their association they met with relevant bodies like the tax policy director and people advising ministers, and met often at MoF over the past few weeks to discuss the issue. “Currently our factories are paying excise tax not only on the production but on the importation of raw material which is affecting the sector,” Ashenafi said.

a4904.speaker: Sources (unnamed)
a4904.speech: According to sources, the excise tax on water products could be calculated on sales as opposed to production in the upcoming proclamation.

a4904.speaker: Government of Ethiopia
a4904.speech: Claimed that even though water is basic and a type of food, bottled water manufacturers affect the environment, and the tax is being imposed to mitigate this.

a4904.speaker: Ashenafi Merid, General Manager of EBWSDMIA
a4904.speech: Said members have agreed to help the environment by collecting wasted plastic and recycling, arguing that “currently industries are working on recycling and some new industries are established to process the plastic to fiber”.

a4904.speaker: Ashenafi Merid, General Manager of EBWSDMIA
a4904.speech: Said that if the tax scheme wasn’t changed some of the factories would be closed, and told Capital that the government representatives have promised the percentage rate would be changed and collected from sales.

a4904.speaker: Ethiopian Bottled Water and Soft Drinks Manufacturing Industries Association (EBWSDMIA)
a4904.speech: “We have conducted our own study showing the stated tax effect on the sector, which employs many people and provides experience to others” ; argued that Kenya and Uganda don’t tax bottled water while Ethiopia’s tax is 20 percent, that the excise tax makes a basic product expensive, and “We insist the government kill the excise tax on water since it is basic for the community. The excise tax on bottled water is calculated on the packaging not on the water.”

a4904.speaker: Food, medicine and health care administration and control proclamation 661/2009 (document)
a4904.speech: In its definition states that “food” means any raw, semi-processed or processed substance for commercial purpose or to be served for the public in any way intended for human consumption that includes water and other drinks, chewing gum, supplementary food and any substance which has been used in the manufacture, preparation or treatment of food, but does not include tobacco and substances used only as medicines.

a5320.speaker: Dr Samia Suluhu Hassan, CCM presidential candidate / President of Tanzania
a5320.speech: Has pledged to boost the economy, build a self-reliant nation, strengthen democracy and good governance for the development of the nation ; said the nation will achieve economic independence by ensuring that every citizen engages in a productive activity ; explained that the government is creating an enabling environment that will allow youth and other Tanzanians to fully participate in economic activities ; “We will ensure that young people stand on their own and become self-reliant. In this way, we will succeed in building both the economy and a strong nation.”

a5320.speaker: Dr Samia Suluhu Hassan, CCM presidential candidate / President of Tanzania
a5320.speech: Added that the nation faced difficult times from 2020 when the world was hit by Covid-19 and Tanzania was heavily affected by aid cuts and reduced international support; noted that the economy shrank during that period, but through strong policies, things have begun to recover ; “Zanzibar has already recorded a 7.1 per cent economic growth rate, while Tanzania now stands at 6 per cent.” ; “Before Covid-19, our economy was growing at 7 per cent, but it dropped during the crisis. With strong economic policies, we have revived our economies. Zanzibar has already achieved strong growth and the Union Government is also performing well. By next year, we will likely hit 7 per cent again.”

a5320.speaker: Dr Samia Suluhu Hassan, CCM presidential candidate / President of Tanzania
a5320.speech: Said the encouraging economic growth has been translated into the implementation of various development projects such as the construction of health facilities, improvements in the education sector, water supply and the electrification of all villages and many hamlets across the country ; added that the government has also managed to build modern markets in different parts of the country, including Zanzibar and to construct roads, bridges and other infrastructure.

a5320.speaker: Dr Samia Suluhu Hassan, CCM presidential candidate / President of Tanzania
a5320.speech: Pledged to maintain and strengthen the Union, describing it as a vital pillar of unity, brotherhood and development for both sides ; “Our Union is 61 years old, that is more than six decades. We pledge to preserve and strongly protect it for the betterment of our nation.” ; “Let us ignore those who belittle the Union.”

a5320.speaker: Dr Samia Suluhu Hassan, CCM presidential candidate / President of Tanzania
a5320.speech: On the blue economy, pledged to continue implementing projects aimed at strengthening the sector, including supporting deep sea fishing activities ; “We have improved marine transport for both people and goods and we will continue to strengthen the sector and build the country’s economy.” ; explained that the government is working on oil and gas initiatives to ensure they benefit the nation.

a5320.speaker: Dr Samia Suluhu Hassan, CCM presidential candidate / President of Tanzania
a5320.speech: Said that if elected, her government would continue to strengthen diplomatic relations, which are essential for maintaining international cooperation and building the national economy ; assured youth, women and people with disabilities that her government would continue to provide them with loans and other forms of support, to boost their livelihoods and promote an inclusive economy.

a5320.speaker: Dr Hussein Mwinyi, Zanzibar’s CCM presidential candidate
a5320.speech: Reminded Zanzibaris to uphold peace and unity; said peace, unity and order are fundamental pillars for building a progressive nation; urged all candidates to promote peace and brotherhood during the campaign period and beyond, stressing that peace is the foundation of every strong government in the world; assured the people of Zanzibar that better days were coming ahead and asked for their support for his re-election on October 29.

a5320.speaker: Dr Asha-Rose Migiro, CCM Secretary General
a5320.speech: Said the Union has been strengthened under the leadership of President Samia and Dr Mwinyi ; “The Union has grown stronger on both sides, including economically.” ; explained that the nation has made economic progress thanks to President Samia’s efforts, including innovative initiatives such as the ‘Royal Tour’ film ; “Through the ‘Royal Tour’ film, Zanzibar and the country as a whole boosted the tourism sector and improved the economy. The film has taken Tanzania to another level in global tourism.” ; “Tourism is an engine of the economy and these improvements have significantly increased tourist numbers and revenue from the sector.”

a5320.speaker: Dr Asha-Rose Migiro, CCM Secretary General
a5320.speech: Noted that Dr Mwinyi has also played a major role in transforming Zanzibar, with many development projects already implemented and more in the pipeline if he is re-elected in October; applauded both President Samia and Dr Mwinyi for investing in education, health, water supply, electricity, markets and other key sectors ; “Dr Mwinyi has so far initiated and implemented many projects. He has been a pillar of development and his strong commitment to building a robust Zanzibar economy is clear.”

a5378.speaker: Emmanuel Armah Kofi Buah, Minister for Lands and Natural Resources
a5378.speech: Has disclosed that about GH¢6.2 billion worth of excavators were imported into the country last year; speaking to journalists in Accra, he wondered the basis for the importation of the large volumes of the excavators if they are not meant for illegal mining businesses.

a5378.speaker: Emmanuel Armah Kofi Buah, Minister for Lands and Natural Resources
a5378.speech: Called on the media to help his ministry fight against illegal mining that is destroying the country's vegetation cover; made a passionate appeal to the media to be vocal and objective in the fight against illegal mining, urging against the politicization of the issue, emphasising the media's role as the fourth estate of the realm and encouraging them to use their platforms to support the government's efforts.

a5378.speaker: Emmanuel Armah Kofi Buah, Minister for Lands and Natural Resources
a5378.speech: According to Armah-Kofi Buah, the attack on Forestry Commission officers exemplifies the composite nature of the problem and underscores the need for inclusive, decisive and radical measures to permanently address the challenge; he disclosed that at the time of the Mahama government's arrival, nine forest reserves in the country were completely under the control of illegal miners, and that the turbidity levels of water treated by the Ghana Water Company Limited ranged from 5,000 to 12,000 NTU, with a vast area comparable to thirty football fields consumed by illegal mining.

a5378.speaker: Emmanuel Armah Kofi Buah, Minister for Lands and Natural Resources
a5378.speech: Stated that the government's anti-galamsey drive is anchored on five key principles: enforcement of existing laws, overhauling of existing structures, intensified stakeholder engagements, deployment of technology, and public sensitization. "We are doing about five things. One, we are strengthening enforcement. Working with law enforcement agents, you will see that enforcement is being intensified." ; "We are making structural changes because, frankly, if a district commander has been at a mining site for five years, it's time for a change. We also have to work with the military." ; "But you know, that is already being intensified. I'm sad to note that efforts were made in the past, but from 2022, the military never entered the forest and that also added to the problem. We've also started engaging chiefs as part of stakeholder engagement." ; "I've talked about technology. We think, as part of this, we must also use technology. The Ministry has established a whole technology sector with monitoring capabilities." ; "In some areas where this has been implemented, it's working very well because we can monitor the areas and see whether an excavator is within its mining area or moving away. We can track and take action. But it has to be expanded. We are also looking at the possibility of deploying technology in forest reserves."

a5378.speaker: Emmanuel Armah Kofi Buah, Minister for Lands and Natural Resources
a5378.speech: Explained that reports from some committees identified the licensing regime in the small-scale mining sector as a major contributor to the thriving galamsey menace; noted that the centralization of the licensing process meant that traditional rulers and District/Municipal and Metropolitan Executives were excluded from the process, which affected their ability to exercise supervisory responsibilities over illegal mining activities.

a5378.speaker: Media practitioners at the engagement
a5378.speech: Commended the Minister for the engagement and efforts so far made and promised to use their platforms to amplify the fight against illegal mining.

a5415.speaker: Jackie K. Phamotse, author of BARE
a5415.speech: “I'm currently completing my communication degree with UNISA. I work as a brand and sales director at Mofaya Beverage Company, which is co-owned by Dj Sbu. I'm also the CEO of a brand rejuvenation company, Phamotse and Company Pty ltd.”

a5415.speaker: Jackie K. Phamotse, author of BARE
a5415.speech: On what inspired the book: “Narrating African stories is my passion and Karabo was a lovely woman. However her life has become a point of reference for many young people. She inspired me to tell the truth of our social ills and challenges. We live in a very brutal yet artificial society and that can come with a huge responsibility. But Karabo's life played out in all our lives and her death opened up a conversation we all fear. Can we value ourselves enough to give up money? Do we love our peace of mind? What does our education system teach us? How do we see signs of abuse? How to we sustain our own lives with out selling our souls? So her life teaches us a lot.”

a5415.speaker: Jackie K. Phamotse, author of BARE
a5415.speech: On the challenges of writing the book: “I self-published BARE, which costs a lot. We've spent over R150 000 on the production of the book, marketing, editing and proofreading, book design and layout. This also includes fees to do research and traveling to our sources. Distribution is also costly, as well as printing the actual copies for bookstores and books for marketing. I ended up using my savings to make this happen. Editors are expensive, as well as the PR team. And the most importing part is getting the right team to help in the growth of the project.”

a5415.speaker: Jackie K. Phamotse, author of BARE
a5415.speech: On what the book is about: “BARE is dedicated to the late Karabo Mokoena, the woman who made news headlines after being burnt to death by her boyfriend. I also delve into Treasure's real life story. She shares the abuse from men that were around her. From her father's power over them, to being gang raped at a club, raped during model castings and how she sold her soul to a man who gave her the lavish lifestyle as he slowly owned her life by taking each piece of her soul. She reveals the truth about what happens behind the high walls of the many businessmen and politicians who strive to make young girls and boys submit to them in order to live the posh lifestyle.” ; “People should work for what they desire and not hand over there dreams to blessers. Hard work and passion can take you far. People should be patient and be willing to learn and grown on their own. Its okay to have challenges and struggle but don't sell your soul.”

a5415.speaker: Jackie K. Phamotse, author of BARE
a5415.speech: On why one should buy the book: “My book is a must-have! It will open people's minds, teach great life lessons, show them a different view to life, most importantly help those who need to be freed from this lifestyle. It will help parents understand what pressures kids face and how can they help. This is a modern day Lifestyle bible!”

a5491.speaker: Water Regulatory Authority of Mozambique (Autoridade Reguladora de Aguas) (official note)
a5491.speech: Announced on Monday a reduction in potable water tariffs across the country, on average 26% in the minimum consumption bracket; explains that the decision was taken on the basis of several factors, notably the need to increase access to the basic water supply service, especially for low-income families ; says it will continue to monitor the public water supply service, in order to create a balance between suppliers and consumers.

a5710.speaker: UAE draft resolution (seen by AFP)
a5710.speech: Calls for "the urgent suspension of hostilities to allow safe and unhindered humanitarian access, and for urgent steps towards a sustainable cessation of hostilities."

a5710.speaker: Lana Zaki Nusseibeh, UAE Ambassador to the UN
a5710.speech: "[Countries] are engaging at the highest level of diplomacy to reach a text that will have impact on the ground. Diplomacy takes time." ; "If this fails, then we will continue to keep trying... There is too much suffering on the ground for the council to continue to fail on this."

a5710.speaker: Diplomatic source (anonymous)
a5710.speech: Said the latest delay was at the request of the United States.

a5710.speaker: Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli Prime Minister
a5710.speech: Said Wednesday there would be no ceasefire in Gaza until the "elimination" of Hamas.

a5710.speaker: Richard Gowan, International Crisis Group analyst
a5710.speech: Said Washington's UN ambassador Linda Thomas-Greenfield "has pitched hard within the US system for a deal" ; "But if the Israelis continue to oppose the resolution, Biden could still decide to block it."

a5710.speaker: Antony Blinken, US Secretary of State
a5710.speech: Would not be drawn on Washington's next move at the Security Council, telling reporters Wednesday that the US was engaging "constructively... to try to resolve some of the issues." ; Said Washington wanted "to make sure that the resolution, in what it calls for and requires, actually advances (humanitarian) effort and doesn't do anything that could actually hurt the delivery of humanitarian assistance."

a5710.speaker: Stephane Dujarric, spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres
a5710.speech: Said it is "not for us to interfere with those discussions, which I understand are fairly intense." ; "The secretary-general's own position is unchanged - he's been calling for a humanitarian ceasefire."

a5985.speaker: Caixa Geral de Depositos (CGD) (statement)
a5985.speech: The state-owned bank said in a statement that the sale of CGD’s 59.81% stake in the capital of Banco Comercial do Atlantico to Coris Holding should be concluded in January.

a5985.speaker: World Bank
a5985.speech: Cabo Verde’s development model was considered exhausted by the World Bank.

a5985.speaker: Olavo Correia, Minister of Finance of Cabo Verde
a5985.speech: Assured on Thursday that the Government is following the entire process of the sale of CGD’s shares in Banco Comercial do Atlantico (BCA) closely and in detail, and rejected the thesis that the sale of BCA may be read as a decline in CGD’s interest in Cabo Verdean banking.

a5985.speaker: Resolution of the Portuguese Council of Ministers
a5985.speech: According to the Council of Ministers Resolution, CGD received three acquisition intentions from among a set of 46 potential investors.

a5985.speaker: Banco Comercial do Atlantico (BCA)
a5985.speech: Reacted to the announcement made by the Union of Workers of Financial Institutions of Cabo Verde (STIF) about a possible strike by BCA workers this year, alleging “unfounded and incorrect statements” that damage the institution’s image.

a5985.speaker: President of the Union of Workers of Financial Institutions of Cabo Verde (STIF)
a5985.speech: Announced today that Banco Comercial do Atlantico (BCA) workers may go on strike, nationwide, “still this year”.

a5985.speaker: Caixa Economica and Banco Comercial do Atlantico
a5985.speech: Announced today the implementation of contingency plans to deal with the new coronavirus pandemic, which involve restrictions on access to branches and placing employees on teleworking.

a5985.speaker: Banco Comercial do Atlantico (BCA) (press statement)
a5985.speech: Issued a statement warning of a ‘phishing’ attempt using “fraudulent e-mails” sent to customers.

a6029.speaker: Elon Musk
a6029.speech: Went as far as calling USAID a "criminal organisation," declaring, "Time for it to die."

a6029.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a6029.speech: Has labeled those in the agency as "radical lunatics."

a6029.speaker: John F. Kennedy, US President (special message to Congress on foreign aid)
a6029.speech: Framed the effort as a strategic necessity, not an act of charity: "There is no escaping our obligations: our moral obligations as a wise leader and good neighbor in the interdependent community of free nations — our economic obligations as the wealthiest people in a world of largely poor people — and our political obligations as the single largest counter to the adversaries of freedom. To fail to meet those obligations now would be disastrous; and, in the long run, more expensive."

a6029.speaker: "Looting Machine" by Tom Burgis (book)
a6029.speech: Lays this out with unsettling clarity: there is no such thing as a vacuum. Resource-rich African nations will not simply be left alone to figure things out ; details the case of President Mamadou Tandja of Niger in its sixth chapter — when he tried to resist the influence of Western-backed financial institutions, other players, most notably China, were quick to step in, offering investment and loans, but on terms that did little to benefit the ordinary Nigerien.

a6281.speaker: Maria Benvinda Levy (Levi), Mozambican Prime Minister
a6281.speech: “If the suspension of external aid from the United States is confirmed, the health sector will be one of the most affected,” Levi told the press during an event in Maputo ; acknowledging that the U.S. support has been crucial, particularly in the health sector, Levi said other areas, with less significant dependence on external aid, might also be impacted.

a6281.speaker: Maria Benvinda Levy (Levi), Mozambican Prime Minister
a6281.speech: Noted that the government is prepared to tackle the challenge despite the significance of the support previously provided. “We have faced other worrying situations before and managed them successfully. I believe this time will be no different, as we will use our internal resources to navigate through.” ; “We will have to redirect some of our resources to ensure these critical areas can continue their activities without disruption,” she added.

a6281.speaker: O Pais (local Mozambican newspaper, Sunday report)
a6281.speech: Reported that in Mozambique more than 400 million U.S. dollars could be affected, which are earmarked annually for the health sector, including 250 million dollars for the HIV program.

a6534.speaker: Michael J. Adler, U.S. Ambassador, and USAID Mission Director Thompson
a6534.speech: Thanked implementing partners for their essential work supporting the South Sudanese people and discussed assistance coordination in South Sudan's challenging humanitarian, security, and economic context.

a6563.speaker: Embassy of the United States of America in Mozambique (press release)
a6563.speech: Confirms, through a press release, the resumption of funding for the Millennium Challenge Corporation programme, valued at more than 500 million dollars in financing for the country, across various reconstruction and social transformation programmes ; The U.S. Embassy guarantees that the programme "is fully aligned with U.S. foreign policy priorities" and that it "aims to produce concrete benefits" for the two peoples.

a6563.speaker: U.S. Embassy press release (the document)
a6563.speech: According to the document, the decision to maintain the programme in Mozambique was taken by the Board of Directors of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) during a meeting that took place in August, which recommended moving forward with Mozambique's Connectivity and Coastal Resilience Compact, within the framework of the review of foreign assistance.

a6563.speaker: Embassy of the United States of America in Mozambique
a6563.speech: According to the Embassy, in this second compact the focus is on improving transport networks in rural areas, under the Rural Transport and Roads Project, which includes the new bridge over the Licungo River and its connecting road; encouraging commercial agriculture through policy and fiscal reforms (Commercial Agriculture Investment Promotion and Reform Project); and strengthening coastal livelihoods through climate resilience initiatives (Livelihoods and Climate Resilience Project).

a6586.speaker: Pakistani authorities
a6586.speech: Said on Friday that gunmen attacked two passenger buses in Pakistan's Balochistan province, before carrying out targeted ethnic killings.

a6586.speaker: Official reports
a6586.speech: According to official reports, buses travelling from the Balochi capital Quetta to Punjab province were stopped in the Zhob and Loralai districts, and gunmen took several passengers off the buses and shot them dead.

a6586.speaker: A survivor from one of the buses (anonymous, speaking to Pakistani daily Dawn)
a6586.speech: "They dragged out 10 passengers — seven from one coach and three from the other — and took them away. I don't know what they did to them, but I heard gunfire as we were leaving."

a6586.speaker: Naveed Alam, government official
a6586.speech: Told reporters that the bodies were recovered in the mountains with bullet wounds.

a6723.speaker: Luísa Meque, chairperson of Mozambique’s National Disaster Management Institute (INGD)
a6723.speech: Announced on Wednesday that at least 1,863 families were affected by cyclone Jude and 908 houses were completely destroyed: “From the preliminary survey carried out, we have six deaths, one in Larde district, another in Meconta district and four in Nacala Port. These are the deaths confirmed by the health authorities. There are twenty injured. This is preliminary data and the teams are still working on the ground. This information will be updated and may change in the next few hours.”

a6723.speaker: Luísa Meque, chairperson of Mozambique’s National Disaster Management Institute (INGD)
a6723.speech: Said, speaking during a session of the Emergency Operations Centre (COE) in Nampula city, that humanitarian assistance for the communities and households affected by Jude is raising concerns due to the condition of the roads: “The rain that accompanied ‘Jude’ caused many access routes to be cut and rivers to burst their banks, flooding various regions” ; “This is a major challenge, therefore we call on the people who are besieged by the rising waters to avoid crossing the rivers. It’s important that they don’t cross without safety, because that could endanger their lives.”

a6723.speaker: Luísa Meque, chairperson of Mozambique’s National Disaster Management Institute (INGD)
a6723.speech: “The frequent occurrence of cyclones in this part of the country, going beyond the meteorological forecasts, is a factor that increases the pressure on the government to provide humanitarian assistance to households, a reality that must be lived with.”

a6723.speaker: Zambezia maritime authorities
a6723.speech: Have ordered all fishermen not to take their boats to sea.

a6768.speaker: Moussa Faki Mahamat, Chairperson of the African Union Commission
a6768.speech: Says Africa must create wealth amongst its people as a tool to curb foreign aid and stimulate peace ; says the need to embrace African ideas on issues facing the continent is also critical to attaining transformation across all spheres of life.

a6768.speaker: Moussa Faki Mahamat, Chairperson of the African Union Commission
a6768.speech: Raised concern about the unconstitutional seizure of political power in Africa, saying although success has been achieved in restoring peace across Africa, concerns still exist; he says at present five African countries are embroiled in post-electoral conflict due to unconstitutional seizures of power, which raises concern as the AU pledged to end armed conflicts by 2020.

a6768.speaker: Moussa Faki Mahamat, Chairperson of the African Union Commission
a6768.speech: In his remarks during a meeting with African diplomats on strategies to restore and maintain peace in Windhoek, emphasised the need to tap into Africa's religious and traditional customs to curb issues of conflict and terrorism.

a6768.speaker: Dr Albert Kawana, Namibia's Minister of Home Affairs, Immigration, Safety and Security
a6768.speech: Expressed optimism about Mahamat's visit to Namibia ; says Namibia remains deeply indebted to the help offered by the world during its quest for independence and will strive by all means to maintain peace and stability in the country.

a6962.speaker: Marcilia Fernandes, President (bastonaria) of the Order of Pharmacists of Cabo Verde
a6962.speech: "It is trade in a health good that can have very serious consequences for people's health. So it is a big problem, indeed, that we have in Cabo Verde," she told Radio de Cabo Verde ; according to the bastonaria, the irregular sale of medicines heightens concern about the rational use of these products, requiring greater intervention by pharmacists in health services.

a6962.speaker: Marcilia Fernandes, President (bastonaria) of the Order of Pharmacists of Cabo Verde
a6962.speech: On public radio, Marcilia Fernandes stressed the importance of the presence of qualified pharmacists in the public sector, especially in health centres and health delegations, which as a rule do not have these professionals. "We have of course been demanding, from the outset, the presence of pharmacists in public health and primary care services," she underlined.

a6962.speaker: Marcilia Fernandes, President (bastonaria) of the Order of Pharmacists of Cabo Verde
a6962.speech: Highlighted the Order's role in the training of professionals, mentioning the recent postgraduate course promoted for hospital-sector pharmacists; however, she reinforced the need to widen the areas of specialisation, covering community pharmacy, regulation and the pharmaceutical industry.

a6962.speaker: Marcilia Fernandes, President (bastonaria) of the Order of Pharmacists of Cabo Verde
a6962.speech: At the end of her second and final term, Marcilia Fernandes assesses the work carried out positively and expresses confidence in the continuity of the projects under way.

a7035.speaker: Imam Alhagie Muhammed Lamin Touray, former President of The Gambia's Supreme Islamic Council
a7035.speech: In his sermon at the inauguration of the Gunjur mosque he preached peace, unity, and stability, and urged Muslims to fulfil their religious obligations with dedication.

a7035.speaker: Imam Alhagie Muhammed Lamin Touray, former President of The Gambia's Supreme Islamic Council
a7035.speech: Expressed profound gratitude to President Barrow for sponsoring the construction, recalled past challenges the community faced in raising funds for a mosque, and said the President had fulfilled their long-held dream: “This singular act will enhance the spiritual development of the community.” He also thanked women, youth, and religious leaders for their support during the project.

a7035.speaker: Chief Falalo Touray and Alkalo Dembo Darboe of Gunjur
a7035.speech: Commended the President, noting that the mosque, together with ongoing road and infrastructure projects, will promote the religious and social development of Gunjur, and urged residents to support the President to enable him to continue his development agenda.

a7035.speaker: Hamat N.K. Bah, Minister of Regional Government, Lands and Religious Affairs
a7035.speech: Described the mosque as one of the most modern in the country, built to meet contemporary architectural standards, and disclosed that President Barrow has funded several mosque projects nationwide, reflecting his commitment to Islam and the spiritual development of Muslims.

a7035.speaker: Hamat N.K. Bah, Minister of Regional Government, Lands and Religious Affairs
a7035.speech: Echoed calls for Gambians to support the President's re-election bid in December, thanked elders and religious leaders for preaching peace and tolerance, and urged them to continue guiding to preserve national tranquillity.

a7035.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a7035.speech: In his inaugural statement thanked the Gunjur community for the honour, noting he had long pledged to support the project; described Gunjur as a historic Islamic settlement that produced renowned scholars including Omar Bun Jeng and Hatab Bojang; said mosques play a vital role in the spiritual and moral development of society; thanked anonymous donors who supported the construction and urged the community to pray for them; called the mosque a progressive project that has changed the infrastructural landscape of Gunjur; and challenged residents to take good care of the mosque and its facilities, pledging government support for its upkeep and maintenance.

a7035.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a7035.speech: On the upcoming December elections, urged Gambians to pray for peace and reassured the nation of the government's commitment to a smooth and credible process: “There are no losers in elections. A peaceful and credible process promotes The Gambia's image as a democratic country.”

a7035.speaker: Saikou Dukureh, Consul General
a7035.speech: Welcomed the President and thanked him for the engagement, described Gambians in Gabon as hardworking, united, and law-abiding, and commended the government for supporting their welfare.

a7035.speaker: Jakarta Dampha, community representative (Gambian community in Gabon)
a7035.speech: Said there has been marked improvement in the well-being of Gambians in Gabon since President Barrow took office, noting that the President's leadership has ensured that Gambians in the diaspora are not discriminated against and that their concerns are addressed promptly.

a7035.speaker: Hawa Dukureh, speaking on behalf of the youth (Gambian community in Gabon)
a7035.speech: Commended the President for dispatching a team of immigration officials to issue national documents, said nearly 200 people were processed, but appealed for support to ensure the passports are delivered.

a7035.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a7035.speech: In his remarks in Libreville expressed gratitude for the warm reception at the airport, which he said even impressed his host, President Oligui Nguema; said dialogue is key to national unity and described it as a great honour to serve as Chief Guest of Honour at Gabon's Independence Anniversary.

a7035.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a7035.speech: On diaspora support, reaffirmed his government's commitment to assisting Gambians abroad, said the decision to send immigration officials to Gabon was to ensure citizens have access to documents, pledged to prioritise the delivery of all processed passports upon his return to Banjul, and advised Gambians seeking repatriation to apply through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for a smooth process.

a7035.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a7035.speech: Updated the community on developments at home, saying the government has laid the foundation stone for 1,500 km of roads across the country and highlighting progress in electricity, health, transport, and education; with the December presidential election approaching, he encouraged those with voter cards to exercise their right and urged those without to encourage family and friends to vote for continuity, and urged the community to maintain unity, peace, and respect for lawful authority.

a7035.speaker: Dr Ahmadou Lamin Samateh, Minister of Health
a7035.speech: Described the new health post in Buduk as “another significant milestone”, reflecting the government's commitment to improving healthcare services.

a7035.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a7035.speech: Said the opening of the Buduk health post aligns with his administration's broader goal of ensuring access to quality healthcare for all Gambians.

a7035.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a7035.speech: Speaking on board the ferry at the start of his nationwide tour, said the tour reflects his government's strategy of delivering social projects directly to ordinary Gambians: “Infrastructure is the foundation upon which all other sectors rely,” describing it as a key pillar of his development agenda.

a7035.speaker: A resident (Fass Njaga Choi, unnamed)
a7035.speech: “This road has been our dream for years. We thank the President for remembering us.”

a7035.speaker: Alhaji Kala Darboe
a7035.speech: Said the new road will create opportunities for women and farmers, while improving access to education, healthcare, and other essential services.

a7035.speaker: Lamin Saidykhan, North Bank Region Governor
a7035.speech: Commended the government for what he described as unprecedented development that has transformed livelihoods in the area, and urged residents to reflect on the impact of these projects on ordinary people.

a7035.speaker: National Assembly Member for the area (Upper Badibou)
a7035.speech: Described the gathering as significant, noting ongoing support for the President in Badibou, which he attributed to the government's track record of delivering roads and health centres, adding that previous administrations had failed to construct the road despite strong local support.

a7035.speaker: Alhaji Jagne, Chief of Central Badibou, and Councillor Maimuna Bah
a7035.speech: Expressed gratitude to the President, recalled past difficulties accessing health facilities due to poor roads, and said patients can now reach care within minutes thanks to the new road, health centre, and provision of ambulances.

a7035.speaker: Fatou Kinteh, Minister of Gender and Children's Welfare
a7035.speech: Said President Barrow's development agenda is visible across all sectors, particularly in women's empowerment, noted that women now hold influential positions in government, and called on women to support the President, adding that Gambian women have pledged to contribute to his nomination fees in December.

a7035.speaker: Sulayman Sumareh, Managing Director of the National Roads Authority
a7035.speech: Disclosed that the Salikenni–Njaba Kunda road is fully government-funded and said the project will improve connectivity and enhance access to health, education, and other social services.

a7035.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a7035.speech: Described the new Salikenni–Banni–Njaba Kunda road as part of his government's plan to connect all communities across the country: “The North Bank Region has received unprecedented attention under this government with the construction of several roads.” He reassured citizens of his administration's commitment to infrastructure and urged communities to take ownership and maintain the projects to serve their intended purpose.

a7035.speaker: Kebba Jallow, former leader of the People's Progressive Party (PPP)
a7035.speech: Reaffirmed his support for President Barrow, saying the President has done so much for the country and deserves another term in office; the delegation pledged to support the President's candidature and work to ensure victory in the December 5th presidential election.

a7035.speaker: Seedy S.K. Njie, Deputy Public Relations Officer of the NPP
a7035.speech: Welcomed the PPP executives into the Alliance and said President Barrow is pleased to accept the endorsement.

a7035.speaker: Gibril Faal, Chief Executive Officer of GK Partners
a7035.speech: Briefed the President on the activities of GK Partners, particularly its ongoing Diaspora Fellowship project being implemented jointly with the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), and updated the President on strides made in diaspora direct investment, noting that The Gambia now leads in monitoring remittance data through the Central Bank of The Gambia.

a7035.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a7035.speech: Underscored his commitment to supporting the GK Partners Diaspora Fellowship project and urged GK Partners to do more public relations work to inform Gambians about their initiatives.

a7145.speaker: Government of Ethiopia
a7145.speech: Announced the impoundment of 4.9 billion cubic metres of water earlier this month - the target for the first filling of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD).

a7145.speaker: Experts and opposition political parties / commentators (Ethiopia)
a7145.speech: Were at the forefront of the chatter over the mediation; the point of overlap for commentators was that Egypt was negotiating in bad faith, with the sole purpose of putting pressure on Ethiopia to accept an unfair deal; there were also concerns of partiality by the mediators for Egypt.

a7145.speaker: Steven Mnuchin, US Treasury Secretary
a7145.speech: "Final testing and filling should not take place without an agreement," Mnuchin wrote in a statement on February 28, 2020.

a7145.speaker: David Malpass, President of the World Bank (Twitter post)
a7145.speech: On June 17, 2020, in a Twitter post where he commented about his communication with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed (PhD) about World Bank financial approvals, added a reminder of the need for Ethiopia to cooperate: "Important [for] Ethiopia and its neighbours to sustain constructive dialogue [and] cooperation on water sharing."

a7145.speaker: Foreign Policy magazine (citing officials and congressional aides familiar with the matter)
a7145.speech: "The Trump administration is weighing withholding some aid to Ethiopia over a Nile dam project that has severely strained its relationship with downstream countries Sudan and Egypt."

a7313.speaker: 2025 Global Report on Food Crises (GRFC)
a7313.speech: Revealed that at least 6.8 million Malawians - over one-third of the population - are unable to meet basic food needs, and that 5.7 million people are classified under IPC Phase 3, a category that signals severe acute food insecurity ; warns that rising poverty and malnourishment are direct consequences of declining welfare, linking this to macroeconomic pressures including foreign exchange shortages, reduced official development assistance, and fragile fiscal capacity: "These factors threaten currency stability and Malawi's ability to import essential goods."

a7313.speaker: Preliminary crop production estimates for the 2024/25 season
a7313.speech: Indicate that Malawi will harvest only 2.96 million metric tonnes of maize against a national requirement of 3.5 million - a shortfall of more than half a million metric tonnes.

a7313.speaker: Leonard Chimwaza, agriculture extension specialist
a7313.speech: Has called for a shift from emergency responses to long-term strategies, recommending prioritizing mega farm productivity, timely input distribution, climate-smart farming, and improved storage infrastructure; he stressed that government must diversify food sources through small-scale livestock farming, and that Admarc's role in ensuring equitable and affordable maize distribution is crucial, especially in the short term.

a7313.speaker: Sam Kawale, Minister of Agriculture
a7313.speech: Acknowledged the gravity of the crisis but pointed to ongoing efforts, revealing that government is investing nearly K100 billion in irrigation projects, with support for fertiliser, seeds, and pest control aimed at boosting off-season production: "We are committed to ensuring no one is left behind. Dodma will continue distributing free food to vulnerable households, and Admarc has received additional funding to sell maize at subsidized prices."

a7407.speaker: Uchizi Mkandawire, Minister of Youths and Sports
a7407.speech: Asked over 1000 TEVETA graduates from Mangochi and Zomba to embrace entrepreneurship in order to create employment for their fellow youths ; said the graduates can reduce unemployment level in the country especially if they start opening up their small scale businesses there by creating self-employment as well as employment for others.

a7407.speaker: Uchizi Mkandawire, Minister of Youths and Sports
a7407.speech: According to Mkandawire, it is President Dr Lazarus Chakwera’s vision to see that many youths are equipped with technical skills and open up their businesses soon after graduation ; said there is a room for those without or with small business capital to obtain a loan from the National Economic Empowerment Fund (NEEF) that President Chakwera initiated.

a7407.speaker: Uchizi Mkandawire, Minister of Youths and Sports
a7407.speech: Thanked the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) for its financial support of the whole initiative through the Titukulane Project: “As government, we want to thank USAID through its Titukulane Project for the initiative because it helped to equip the Youths with different technical skills. And to the graduates, please go and embrace entrepreneurship.”

a7407.speaker: Elwin Sichiola, TEVETA executive director
a7407.speech: In his remarks, while thanking USAID, said the country needs to have more programs like the Titukulane Project.

a7439.speaker: Rev. William Hybels, founder and Senior Pastor of Willow Creek Community Church, South Barrington, Illinois, USA
a7439.speech: "The Church is the hope of the world, and leaders of the Church are the hope of the Church."

a7439.speaker: Liberian Council of Churches (LCC) (initial statement)
a7439.speech: Issued an initial statement condemning the current crisis within the United Methodist Church, Liberia Annual Conference and calling on all engaging parties to cease the confrontations and public outbursts and dialogue.

a7439.speaker: Rev. Dr. Slewion P. Lewis, Ordained Priest of the Episcopal Church of Liberia (author)
a7439.speech: Calls on the leadership of the governing body of the Church in Liberia to take more visible and concrete actions in resolving the conflict within the United Methodist Church, Liberia Annual Conference in order to restore peace within that part of the Body of Christ and bring dignity to the Church in Liberia; urges that leaders of the Church rise above the feud and put the interest of the Church and the work of God above their individual interests, and that they settle disputes outside social media and the public so as not to bring the Church to public ridicule and embarrassment.

a7461.speaker: Document sighted by Daily Trust / Motor Tanker vessels report
a7461.speech: Showed that the product arrived into the country on Monday, 10th February; indicated that NNPCL spent over N126.5 billion to import more than 136.7 million litres of PMS in a single day, importing 102,000 metric tonnes of PMS on Monday, 10th February; showed that 37,000 metric tonnes were transported by the Kriti Bay and Kouris ships via the ASPM terminal, while another 28,000 metric tonnes were brought in by the Hapnia Andre ship through the PWA/BOP/NOJ terminal.

a7461.speaker: NNPC (Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited)
a7461.speech: Announced in December 2024 the resumption of refining operation for the 125,000 barrels per day Warri Refinery and Petrochemical Company (WRPC).

a7461.speaker: Some stakeholders and industry players
a7461.speech: Said Nigeria should not be importing this much if truly the government refineries are now working.

a7461.speaker: A source (anonymous industry source)
a7461.speech: "Besides why are we importing this much when our daily consumption is just 30 million litres. We really need to probe this to really have a true picture of what is happening."

a7461.speaker: Another industry player (anonymous)
a7461.speech: "There is a lot that is not true. You all don't question anything coming from the refineries. You think everything is true?"

a7461.speaker: Dr. Ayodele Oni, energy expert
a7461.speech: Said given recent advancements in domestic refining capabilities, highlighted by the operational or near-operational status of refineries at Dangote, Port Harcourt, and Warri, this situation sparks concerns: "By February 2025, the Dangote refinery, designed for 650,000 barrels daily, is functioning at 85% and aims for full capacity within a month. Active since September 2024, it's producing various fuels, including pms (colloquially referred to as petrol). However, local crude oil access issues compel temporary fuel imports for its operation." ; "Regarding Port Harcourt and Warri, the official announcement about the kickoff of operations at Port Harcourt (210,000 barrels per day) and Warri (125,000 barrels per day) promised a combined 335,000 barrels daily output. Yet, their operational efficiency seems troubled." ; "Despite the presence of these three refineries, operational challenges persistently hinder their output effectiveness. Steady access to crude oil remains problematic; for example, the Dangote Refinery's struggle to source adequate local crude has necessitated temporary imports. Additional factors prompting this include market forces, demand dynamics, and existing contractual commitments." ; "Ultimately, while these fuel imports raise issues, it's critical to comprehensively assess Nigeria's fuel production capabilities, the current demand, and whether NNPCL's strategy offers a more viable solution."

a7461.speaker: Ajani Monsuru, a commercial driver
a7461.speech: Said the reduction is not significant, adding that motorists would only see relief when fuel prices crash below N900.

a7493.speaker: Christine Fossen, Police Commissioner for the UN Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS)
a7493.speech: Thanked them for their dedicated service to protect civilians and to support the SSNPS capacity development. “Your medals represent a personal sacrifice you have made as part of our joint endeavour to protect civilians and sustain durable peace in this country of South Sudan.” ; “You are almost at the end of your mission and receiving these medals is indeed an important milestone in your deployment.”

a7493.speaker: Commissioner of Police (CP) Felly Rutagerura Bahizi, UNMISS Chief of Operations
a7493.speech: Thanked the decorated officers’ determination and contribution to peace efforts in South Sudan.

a7493.speaker: Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Angelique Uwamariya, RWAFPU-3 contingent commander
a7493.speech: Thanked UNMISS for the support in the execution of their mandate. “We contributed to the protection of civilians, creating conditions that are conducive to the delivery of humanitarian assistance, monitoring and investigating human rights violations as well as supporting the implementation of revitalized agreement and peace process.” She added that the RWAFPU 3-6 trained the South Sudan Police on public order management, Police techniques, and tactics such as arrest and detention methods, and also thanked the officers under her command for their professionalism, commitment, and hard work to fulfill the UNMISS mandate, despite the challenges.
